items.title: Automated migrate-then-deploy pipeline with per-tenant schema versions and an expand/contract policy

labels.name: priority: P1-high
labels.description: Blocks scaling to more tenants or real user pain

labels.name: status: needs-input
labels.description: Needs a decision, info or access from the owner before work starts

labels.name: source: audit-2026-10
labels.description: Found in the October 2026 architecture/security/UX audit

items.body:
## Problem
Schema rollout is a manual step from a laptop. Vercel's Git integration deploys `main` on push whether or not migrations ran, so new code can hit an old schema, and a forgotten tenant stays behind. Nothing links a commit to the schema version it needs.

## Evidence
- README: "Vor einem Deploy mit Schemaänderungen zuerst migrieren" (`pnpm db:control:migrate`, then `pnpm db:migrate-tenants`).
- No `vercel.json` and no `.github/`, so production deploys come only from Vercel Git auto-deploy.
- Migrations are applied straight to production with no backup anchor (`scripts/migrate-tenants.ts:170-181`).

## Proposal
Expand/contract policy, enforced by the migration checks:
- **Release N (expand):** additive only (new tables, nullable or defaulted columns). `drizzle/0011_feature_settings.sql` is a good example. Old code must keep working on the new schema.
- **Release N+1:** code stops using the old shape.
- **Release N+2 (contract):** `DROP`/`RENAME`, labelled `migration:contract`, only after all tenants are on N+1.

Turn off Git auto-deploy for production only, so GitHub Actions is the single path to prod and previews keep deploying:
```json
{ "git": { "deploymentEnabled": { "main": false } } }
```
```yaml
# .github/workflows/release.yml
name: Release
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
concurrency:
  group: production
  cancel-in-progress: false
jobs:
  ci:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/ci.yml
  migrate:
    needs: ci
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production   # required reviewer + prod secrets live here only
    env:
      SKIP_ENV_VALIDATION: '1'
      BETTER_AUTH_URL: https://rhenania-stuttgart.de
      CONTROL_DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.CONTROL_DATABASE_URL }}
      CONTROL_DATABASE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CONTROL_DATABASE_AUTH_TOKEN }}
      DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}
      DATABASE_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DATABASE_AUTH_TOKEN }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 24, cache: pnpm }
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm db:migrate-tenants --dry-run
      - run: echo "PITR anchor $(date -u +%FT%TZ)" >> $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY
      - run: pnpm db:control:migrate
      - run: pnpm db:migrate-tenants --tenant=rhenania   # canary
      - run: pnpm db:migrate-tenants
  deploy:
    needs: migrate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    env:
      VERCEL_ORG_ID: ${{ secrets.VERCEL_ORG_ID }}
      VERCEL_PROJECT_ID: ${{ secrets.VERCEL_PROJECT_ID }}
      VERCEL_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.VERCEL_TOKEN }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 24, cache: pnpm }
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm dlx vercel@latest pull --yes --environment=production --token=$VERCEL_TOKEN
      - run: pnpm dlx vercel@latest build --prod --token=$VERCEL_TOKEN
      - run: pnpm dlx vercel@latest deploy --prebuilt --prod --token=$VERCEL_TOKEN
      - run: curl -fsS https://rhenania-stuttgart.de/api/health
```
Rollback means rolling back code with `vercel rollback`. Schema is never auto-reversed; because of expand/contract, old code still works.

## Acceptance criteria
- Merging to `main` runs CI, then migrations (control, canary, all tenants), then deploy, then the smoke test.
- A failed migration blocks the deploy.
- README documents expand/contract and the rollback runbook.

## Open questions
- Vercel and GitHub access: who creates `VERCEL_TOKEN` and the `production` environment with a required reviewer?
- Is turning off production Git auto-deploy acceptable?
- Should the `migrate` job be skipped when `drizzle/**` is unchanged (paths filter)?

<details><summary>Also reported by the Architecture review: Move tenant migrations into CI with per-tenant schema versions and stop prod drift (db:push, max(created_at) skips, --repair)</summary>

## Problem
Schema changes reach tenants through a laptop script run with production credentials. Nothing ties a migration run to a deploy, and there is no record of which schema version each tenant is on.

Drizzle's migrator treats any journal entry with `when <= max(created_at)` as applied. A single out-of-order or hand-inserted row therefore makes later migrations skip forever without an error. That already happened to Hassia.

`--repair` swallows `already exists` errors and records the migration as applied, which can mask partial or divergent schemas. `drizzle.config.ts` points `db:push` at the production Rhenania DB.

The tenants are migrated one at a time and the run keeps going after failures. With 200 tenants and one deployed code version, a single run can leave the fleet on mixed schemas.

## Evidence
- `scripts/migrate-tenants.ts:60-74` (max(created_at) logic), `:79-119` (repair swallow), `:147-190` (sequential, continue on failure).
- `scripts/repair-hassia-journal.ts:3-6` (hand-inserted rows blocked 0001-0005).
- `drizzle/control/meta/_journal.json`: `idx` jumps 3 → 5 (0004 missing), and `scripts/apply-control-migration-0005.ts` exists.
- `package.json:18,23` (`db:push`, `db:control:push`). `drizzle.config.ts:9-12` targets `DATABASE_URL`.
- `src/server/lib/tenant-context.ts:96-111`: runtime code tolerates the control migration "hasn't run yet", which is evidence of deploy/migrate ordering races.
- There is no `.github/` directory, and there are 24 one-off scripts in `scripts/`.

## Proposal
1. Add a `control_tenant_schema` row (tenantId, appliedTag, appliedAt, status).
2. Add a CI job (GitHub Actions, running before Vercel promotion) that:
   - verifies journal `when` values are strictly increasing;
   - runs migrations against a fresh libSQL file;
   - fans out to tenants with bounded concurrency (e.g. 10);
   - records versions and blocks promotion on any failure.
3. Adopt expand/contract: code must work with schema N-1. A deploy goes out only after expand migrations have run on 100% of tenants.
4. Delete the `db:push` scripts from `package.json`, and make `--repair` require `--tenant` and print a diff against `sqlite_master`.
5. Show schema versions in /superadmin.

## Acceptance criteria
- A deploy cannot go live with a tenant behind.
- Journal monotonicity is checked in CI.
- /superadmin lists every tenant's schema tag.
- `pnpm db:push` no longer exists.

## Open questions
- Where may CI hold production Turso and control credentials (GitHub environment secrets vs. a Vercel build step)?
- Is a short maintenance window acceptable for contract migrations?

</details>

items.title: Production mode never runs the runtime's boot-time DDL, so a production DB drifts from a development one (search_vector, dazzle_files.uploaded_by, _dazzle_usage_events)
items.body:
## What we found

On Dazzle v0.123.0 (`b29c0258`), with `DAZZLE_ENV=production` and the schema managed by the Alembic chain (release phase runs `dazzle db upgrade head`), diffing production's tables and columns against a database built from nothing to the same Alembic head (`dazzle db upgrade head` on an empty DB, then the app booted once in development mode) shows objects that exist only where a development boot has happened:

| Object | Created by | On a production-mode DB |
|---|---|---|
| `CohortAssessment.search_vector` (generated tsvector) + its GIN index | `dazzle/http/runtime/search_schema.py` (`ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS search_vector …`, run after `metadata.create_all`) | missing |
| `dazzle_files.uploaded_by` | `dazzle/http/runtime/file_storage.py:352` (`ALTER TABLE dazzle_files ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS uploaded_by TEXT`) | missing |
| `_dazzle_usage_events` (+ indexes) | `dazzle/http/runtime/usage_signal.py:45` (`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`) | missing |
| `_dazzle_events`, `_dazzle_dlq`, `_dazzle_consumer_offsets`, `devices` | runtime / `framework_tables.py` | present (created earlier, before we switched to production mode) |

So a DSL `search:` spec, the file store's uploader column and the usage signal depend on DDL that only a development-mode boot applies. Production mode (rightly) runs no boot-time DDL, and nothing in the Alembic chain (`0001_framework_baseline` … `0027_two_factor_restore`) creates these objects, so a production database silently lacks them for ever. The same class of drift bit this project in May (ADR-0010: `create_all` never added columns).

## What we would like

One of:

1. Framework Alembic migrations for everything the runtime otherwise creates at boot (`_dazzle_usage_events`, `dazzle_files.uploaded_by`, the event/dlq/offset tables, `devices`), so a production-mode DB at head has them; and for search, a migration helper the project can call (or `dazzle db upgrade` applying `build_search_index_ddl` for the spec's `search:` entities as a post-upgrade step, since the generated column's expression comes from the DSL).
2. Or a `dazzle db sync-runtime-schema` command that applies exactly the runtime's idempotent `IF NOT EXISTS` DDL to a target DB, callable from a release phase.

Either way a `dazzle db verify` (or `dazzle db check`) that reports "runtime objects missing on this DB" would let a release gate catch it.

## How we see it today

Project-side we now run a normaliser after every deploy (`pipeline/db/normalise.py` in cyfutureuk/aegismark) that diffs prod's `information_schema.columns` against a head-migrated reference DB; it is what reported the three rows above. Happy to test a fix on our pin bump.

items.title: Implement the tenant-data export pipeline (ITenantDataExporter)
items.body:
> [!NOTE]
> Filed from issue packet in [HoneyDrunk.Architecture](https://github.com/HoneyDrunkStudios/HoneyDrunk.Architecture).
> Packet: `generated/issue-packets/active/adr-0050-tenant-lifecycle/06-data-tenant-data-export-pipeline.md` · ADRs: ADR-0050 · Initiative: adr-0050-tenant-lifecycle

# Implement the tenant-data export pipeline (ITenantDataExporter)

## Summary
Implement the ADR-0050 D7 data export contract in `HoneyDrunk.Data`: the `ITenantDataExporter` contract in `HoneyDrunk.Data.Abstractions`, a runtime that walks tenant-scoped repositories filtering by `TenantId` per ADR-0026's primitives, emits NDJSON + CSV + manifest.json + schema/*.json + README.md into a ZIP archive, uploads the ZIP to Azure Blob Storage, and returns a 7-day signed URL. Rate-limited to one export per tenant per 24 hours per D7. Audited via `TenantDataExported` event. Version-bumping packet for `HoneyDrunk.Data`.

## Context
ADR-0050 D7 commits the data export contract. Customers own their data; offboarding (and any point in the lifecycle) must produce a complete export. The format is a ZIP archive containing:
- `manifest.json` — version, tenant ID, export timestamp, included tables, record counts, schema version.
- `data/*.json` — NDJSON, one record per line, one file per logical entity type.
- `data/*.csv` — parallel CSV per relevant table, for non-developer-friendly inspection.
- `schema/*.json` — JSON schema documents for each entity type.
- `README.md` — explains the structure, schema versions, format guarantees.

**Scope (per D7):** tenant-scoped data only. The audit substrate is excluded (tenant is not the controller; audit holds pseudonymous tokens anyway). Pulse / Observe telemetry is excluded. Stripe billing records are excluded (customer can export from Stripe directly).

**Delivery:** a signed Azure Blob Storage URL, valid for 7 days. Trigger is self-serve via the tenant portal (eventually — this packet ships the export pipeline; the portal-facing trigger is a deferred follow-up Studios change). Rate limit: **one export per tenant per 24 hours.**

**Per the dispatch plan,** the export walks tenant-scoped repositories filtering by `TenantId` per ADR-0026's primitives (which exist today). It does NOT assume a particular per-tenant partition layout — when a Tenant-Data-Isolation ADR lands (currently absent; cited in ADR-0050 as "ADR-0049" but that citation is an error), the export contract is partition-agnostic and the implementation can grow partition-awareness behind the same surface.

`HoneyDrunk.Data` is a live Node at v0.6.0 (per the active-initiatives.md and overview doc). This packet is the **first packet on the `HoneyDrunk.Data` solution in this initiative** — per invariant 27 it bumps every non-test `.csproj` to the same new minor version (`0.6.0` → `0.7.0`; new feature: the export pipeline; additive).

> **Hybrid sync/async note (per ADR-0050 D7 alternatives section).** D7 alternatives discuss synchronous-only vs hybrid sync/async delivery. The v1 path is **hybrid**: for small exports (under a partition-size threshold, decided at implementation time — start with 10 MB compressed estimate), generate the ZIP synchronously and return the signed URL inline. For larger exports, queue the export work, return immediately, and email the tenant owner the signed URL when generation completes. This packet ships the synchronous path; the async/email path is **deferred to a follow-up packet** because the async path requires (a) a queue substrate, (b) an email-on-export-complete template in `HoneyDrunk.Communications`, and (c) decisions about how the queue work is scheduled. The sync-only path is fine for v1 — partition sizes are small at v1 volume.

## Scope

### `HoneyDrunk.Data.Abstractions` — new contracts
- `ITenantDataExporter` — interface:
  - `ValueTask<TenantExportResult> ExportAsync(TenantId tenant, PseudoUserToken requestingUser, CancellationToken ct)` — generates the export, uploads to Blob, returns a result carrying the signed URL.
- `TenantExportResult` — record carrying: the signed URL, the URL's expiration timestamp (T+7 days), the export's blob name, the record-count summary (one count per entity type exported), the total uncompressed bytes, the total compressed bytes, the export timestamp.
- `TenantExportEntry` — record describing one logical entity type included in the export: entity-type name, table/repository name, record count, schema version.
- `TenantExportManifest` — record describing the manifest.json contents: schema version (start at `"1"`), tenant ID, export timestamp, included entries, requesting user token, total record count.
- `ITenantExportRateLimiter` — interface:
  - `ValueTask<bool> TryAcquireAsync(TenantId tenant, CancellationToken ct)` — returns true if the tenant has not exported in the last 24 hours; false otherwise.
- `TenantExportRateLimitException` — thrown when the rate limit is exceeded; the message names the next-allowed-at timestamp.

### `HoneyDrunk.Data` (runtime) — implementations
- `TenantDataExporter` implementation. Walks tenant-scoped repositories via the existing `IRepository<T>` / `IUnitOfWork` surface, filtering by `TenantId`. For each registered entity type:
  - Streams NDJSON to a temp file.
  - Streams CSV to a temp file (skipping nested/complex types that don't flatten cleanly — document the rule).
  - Generates the JSON schema for the type into a temp file.
- Builds `manifest.json` from `TenantExportManifest`.
- Generates `README.md` from a static template (the structure description, schema-version notes, format guarantees).
- ZIPs everything (`System.IO.Compression.ZipArchive`).
- Uploads the ZIP to Azure Blob Storage at a tenant-scoped path: `exports/{tenant_id}/{export_timestamp_ulid}.zip`.
- Generates a SAS (Shared Access Signature) URL valid for 7 days from generation, with read-only permissions.
- Returns a `TenantExportResult`.

In-memory `ITenantExportRateLimiter` default (mirrors the in-memory pattern across the Grid); a real implementation would use a small Cosmos/SQL table — deferred follow-up.

### Audit emission

The export emits a `TenantDataExported` audit event via `IAuditLog.Append(AuditEntry.CreatePseudonymous(..., AuditEvents.TenantDataExported, ...))` with the tenant's `PseudoTenantToken` and the requesting user's `PseudoUserToken`. Metadata: blob name, record-count summary, success/failure outcome. **This packet's audit emission is direct from the exporter** (the exporter has the tokens in hand — they're passed in to `ExportAsync` — and is composing audit at the natural boundary). Alternative routing through `HoneyDrunk.Communications` is unnecessary here: the export is a deterministic, single-shot operation, not an orchestrated cross-Node workflow.

### Configuration
- The Azure Blob Storage account / container name for exports — config-time. Default container name: `tenant-exports`.
- The signed-URL TTL — config-time, default 7 days (T+7 per D7).
- The rate-limit window — config-time, default 24 hours per tenant.

### Versioning
- Bump every non-test `.csproj` in the `HoneyDrunk.Data` solution to `0.7.0` in one commit (invariant 27).
- Repo-level `CHANGELOG.md` new `[0.7.0]` entry.
- `HoneyDrunk.Data.Abstractions/CHANGELOG.md` `[0.7.0]` entry.
- `HoneyDrunk.Data/CHANGELOG.md` `[0.7.0]` entry.
- READMEs updated.

## Proposed Implementation

### 1. Walking tenant-scoped repositories

The Grid's existing tenant-scoping primitive is `TenantId` per ADR-0026. Tenant-scoped repositories filter by `TenantId` already (per the existing `IRepository<T>` patterns). The exporter:

- Accepts a registered list of `ITenantExportableEntity` descriptors (entity-type name, repository accessor, schema version). The host registers each tenant-scoped entity it wants included.
- For each descriptor, calls `repository.Query().Where(e => e.TenantId == tenant).AsAsyncEnumerable()` (or the equivalent in the repository's API).
- Serializes each entity as NDJSON (one JSON object per line, `\n` terminator).
- Generates a CSV with a header row matching the entity's public properties; nested complex types serialize as JSON-stringified columns; nullable fields are blank cells.
- Generates the entity's JSON schema (using `System.Text.Json.Schema` or a similar generator).

The list of exportable entities **is empty in v1** — the contract surface exists, the runtime works, but no entity is registered out of the box because no Grid Node has tenant-scoped data yet (Auth's `Tenant` table is tenant-metadata, not tenant data the tenant owns; Communications' Prospect / decision-log records are operational, not tenant-owned). When Notify gains tenant-scoped message records, or when Billing scaffolds with tenant-scoped invoice records, those Nodes register their export descriptors via `services.AddTenantExportDescriptor<MessageRecord>(...)`.

The empty-export case (no descriptors registered) is acceptable and a tested code path: the manifest is empty, the ZIP contains only `manifest.json` + `README.md` ("No tenant-owned entities were exportable at this time. This is correct for the current Grid configuration."), the signed URL is still returned.

### 2. The ZIP layout

```
{export_timestamp_ulid}.zip
├── manifest.json
├── README.md
├── data/
│   ├── {entity-type-1}.ndjson
│   ├── {entity-type-1}.csv
│   ├── {entity-type-2}.ndjson
│   ├── {entity-type-2}.csv
│   └── ...
└── schema/
    ├── {entity-type-1}.schema.json
    ├── {entity-type-2}.schema.json
    └── ...
```

### 3. The signed URL

Use `Azure.Storage.Blobs` SDK to generate a SAS URL with:
- Read-only permission.
- 7-day expiration from generation.
- The SAS is generated using the account's user-delegation key (preferred) or the account key — config-time decision.

### 4. Rate limiting

```csharp
public async ValueTask<TenantExportResult> ExportAsync(TenantId tenant, PseudoUserToken requestingUser, CancellationToken ct)
{
    if (!await _rateLimiter.TryAcquireAsync(tenant, ct))
        throw new TenantExportRateLimitException(
            tenant,
            nextAllowedAt: /* now + remaining window */);

    // ... generate the export
}
```

The in-memory rate limiter is a simple `ConcurrentDictionary<TenantId, DateTimeOffset>` of last-export timestamps; if `now - lastExport < 24h`, return false.

### 5. Audit emission

After upload succeeds:

```csharp
var auditEntry = AuditEntry.CreatePseudonymous(
    id: AuditEntryId.New(),
    occurredAt: DateTimeOffset.UtcNow,
    actor: requestingUser,
    tenantToken: /* resolved from IIdentityMap by tenant id */,
    eventName: AuditEvents.TenantDataExported,
    category: AuditCategory.Action,
    outcome: AuditOutcome.Succeeded,
    target: new AuditTarget(...),
    metadata: new Dictionary<string, string>
    {
        ["blob_name"] = blobName,
        ["record_count"] = totalRecords.ToString(),
        ["compressed_bytes"] = compressedBytes.ToString(),
    });

await _auditLog.Append(auditEntry);
```

The tenant's `PseudoTenantToken` is resolved via `IIdentityMap.ResolveTenantAsync(tenant)` — packet 03's Auth-side `IIdentityMap` is wired here (TenantDataExporter takes `IIdentityMap` as a constructor dependency).

If the export *fails* (storage upload error, etc.), emit a `TenantDataExported` event with `AuditOutcome.Failed` and the failure reason in metadata. The audit substrate gets the record of attempted-and-failed; the exception is rethrown to the caller.

### 6. Tests

- Happy path with one registered entity: export runs, ZIP contains manifest + README + data + schema files for the entity, signed URL returned, audit event emitted.
- Empty-export path (no descriptors registered): ZIP contains manifest (empty entries array) + README explaining the empty result, signed URL still returned, audit event emitted.
- Rate-limit path: second export within 24 hours throws `TenantExportRateLimitException`; no audit event emitted (or an audit event with `Failed` outcome — implementation choice, document in tests).
- Failure path: storage upload fails; exception rethrown; audit event emitted with `Failed` outcome.
- NDJSON shape: each line is valid JSON; line count matches record count.
- CSV shape: header row matches entity properties; row count = record count + 1 (header).
- Manifest shape: entries list matches the descriptors that ran; record counts match the actual data.

## Affected Files
- `src/HoneyDrunk.Data.Abstractions/TenantExport/` — new folder with contracts (ITenantDataExporter, TenantExportResult, TenantExportEntry, TenantExportManifest, ITenantExportRateLimiter, TenantExportRateLimitException, ITenantExportableEntity)
- `src/HoneyDrunk.Data/TenantExport/` — new folder with implementations (TenantDataExporter, InMemoryTenantExportRateLimiter, ZipExportWriter, the manifest-builder, the README template)
- `src/HoneyDrunk.Data/DependencyInjection/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs` (extended — `AddHoneyDrunkTenantExport`, `AddTenantExportDescriptor<T>`)
- Every non-test `.csproj` — version bump to `0.7.0`
- `src/HoneyDrunk.Data.Abstractions/CHANGELOG.md`, `README.md`
- `src/HoneyDrunk.Data/CHANGELOG.md`, `README.md`
- Repo-level `CHANGELOG.md`
- Test project(s) — the tests listed above

## NuGet Dependencies
- **`HoneyDrunk.Data.Abstractions`** — gain `HoneyDrunk.Auth.Abstractions` v0.6.0 (for `IIdentityMap` — used by the exporter to resolve the tenant token) and `HoneyDrunk.Audit.Abstractions` v0.2.0 (for `PseudoUserToken`, `PseudoTenantToken`, `AuditEvents`). The existing `HoneyDrunk.Kernel.Abstractions` is retained.
- **`HoneyDrunk.Data`** (runtime) — gain `Azure.Storage.Blobs` (latest stable, currently 12.x — confirm at execution time). Transitively gains the above Abstractions.
- Confirm exact versions at execution time — packets 02 and 03 set them.

## Boundary Check
- [x] The export pipeline is **persistence and data-shape**, not orchestration. It belongs in `HoneyDrunk.Data` per the existing patterns (`IRepository<T>`, `IUnitOfWork`, the outbox). Routing rule "persistence, repository, tenant data, ... → HoneyDrunk.Data" maps exactly.
- [x] The signed-URL emission uses Azure Blob Storage; this is the existing pattern for Grid-internal blob handling (per `HoneyDrunk.Data` conventions). No new vendor.
- [x] Audit emission goes through `IAuditLog.Append` with `AuditEntry.CreatePseudonymous` from packet 02 — preserves invariant 47 (audit append-only) and satisfies invariant 78 (pseudonymous tokens only).
- [x] Tenant-scoping uses ADR-0026's `TenantId` primitive — preserves invariant 39 (tenant mechanics at intake/post-dispatch boundaries).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `HoneyDrunk.Data.Abstractions` exposes `ITenantDataExporter` with `ExportAsync(TenantId, PseudoUserToken, CancellationToken)`
- [ ] `HoneyDrunk.Data.Abstractions` exposes `TenantExportResult`, `TenantExportEntry`, `TenantExportManifest`, `ITenantExportRateLimiter`, `TenantExportRateLimitException`, `ITenantExportableEntity`
- [ ] `HoneyDrunk.Data` ships `TenantDataExporter` implementation: walks registered tenant-scoped entities filtering by `TenantId`, emits NDJSON + CSV + JSON schema per entity, builds manifest.json + README.md, ZIPs everything, uploads to Azure Blob Storage, returns a 7-day signed URL
- [ ] Rate limit: a second export within 24 hours throws `TenantExportRateLimitException` naming the next-allowed timestamp
- [ ] Audit emission: every export (success or failure) emits a `TenantDataExported` event via `IAuditLog.Append(AuditEntry.CreatePseudonymous(...))` using the tenant's `PseudoTenantToken` (resolved via `IIdentityMap`) and the requesting user's `PseudoUserToken`
- [ ] Empty-export path (no registered entities) returns a valid manifest with empty entries list + README explaining the empty result + a signed URL — does not throw
- [ ] DI extensions `AddHoneyDrunkTenantExport()` and `AddTenantExportDescriptor<T>()` register the exporter and the per-entity descriptors
- [ ] Configuration carries the Blob storage account/container name and the signed-URL TTL (default 7 days)
- [ ] All new public types have XML documentation (invariant 13)
- [ ] Every non-test `.csproj` in the solution is at `0.7.0` in a single commit (invariant 27)
- [ ] Repo-level `CHANGELOG.md` has a new `[0.7.0]` entry
- [ ] `HoneyDrunk.Data.Abstractions/CHANGELOG.md` and `HoneyDrunk.Data/CHANGELOG.md` have `[0.7.0]` entries
- [ ] READMEs updated to document the export contract
- [ ] Tests cover happy path, empty-export, rate limit, failure-with-audit, NDJSON shape, CSV shape, manifest shape
- [ ] Tests contain no `Thread.Sleep` (invariant 51)
- [ ] The `pr-core.yml` tier-1 gate passes

## Human Prerequisites
- [ ] **Azure Blob Storage container exists for tenant exports** — a `tenant-exports` container in a Grid-shared or Data-owned Storage Account (`sthd{purpose}{env}` per Grid naming). Free tier is fine for v1 (object count and TTL are both small).
- [ ] **SAS user-delegation key configured (preferred) OR account key seeded in Vault** — the runtime needs credentials to generate signed URLs. User-delegation-key with the Data Node's Managed Identity is the preferred path (per ADR-0006 Vault-namespaced secrets); account-key in the Data Node's Vault namespace is the fallback. The choice is implementation-time.
- [ ] **Blob lifecycle rule for the export container** — set up a 30-day lifecycle rule to auto-delete exports older than 30 days. Exports are short-lived signed-URL-accessed artifacts; permanent retention is wasted storage. Configure in the portal under Storage Account → Lifecycle management. Cost: negligible at v1 volume.
- [ ] No Studios portal change in this packet — the customer-facing "Download my data" trigger is a deferred follow-up tied to the eventual Studios admin console + tenant portal work.

## Referenced ADR Decisions

**ADR-0050 D7 — Data export contract.** ZIP archive with manifest.json + data/*.ndjson + data/*.csv + schema/*.json + README.md. Tenant-scoped data only — audit, telemetry, Stripe records are explicitly excluded. Signed Azure Blob URL valid for 7 days. Self-serve trigger (eventually via tenant portal — deferred). Rate-limited to one export per tenant per 24 hours. Audited via `TenantDataExported` event referencing pseudonymous tokens.

**ADR-0050 D5 — Offboarding-window exports.** During the 30-day Offboarding grace window, the tenant portal remains accessible for export purposes only. This packet ships the export pipeline; the offboarding-window-specific portal path is a deferred follow-up.

**ADR-0050 D7 alternatives — Sync-only vs hybrid sync/async delivery.** v1 ships synchronous-only; async/email path is a deferred follow-up.

**ADR-0026 — `TenantId` primitive (referenced).** The export walks repositories filtering by `TenantId`. Tenant-scoping mechanics are unchanged.

**ADR-0050 D6 — `TenantDataExported` audit event uses pseudonymous tokens.** Tenant's `PseudoTenantToken` (resolved via `IIdentityMap.ResolveTenantAsync`); requesting user's `PseudoUserToken`. The audit substrate carries the operational record without PII; invariants 47 and 78 are preserved.

**Invariant 27 (constraint) — Solution-wide version bump.** `0.6.0 → 0.7.0` for `HoneyDrunk.Data` in one commit.

**Invariant 39 (referenced) — Tenant mechanics at intake/post-dispatch boundaries.** The exporter is a post-dispatch operation; tenant resolution + filter happens at the exporter's entry, not in shared dispatch paths.

**Invariant 47 (referenced) — Audit substrate is append-only.** `TenantDataExported` event uses `IAuditLog.Append` (append-only).

**Invariant 78 (this initiative) — Audit substrate accepts only pseudonymous tokens.** The export's audit emission uses `AuditEntry.CreatePseudonymous` with `PseudoTenantToken` + `PseudoUserToken`.

## Constraints
- **Tenant-scoped data only.** The export must NOT include the audit substrate, Pulse/Observe telemetry, Stripe records, or any data the tenant is not the controller for. This is a load-bearing privacy / boundary commitment — the test suite must verify the exclusions explicitly.
- **The exportable-entity registry is empty by default.** No registered descriptors out of the box. Hosts compose `services.AddTenantExportDescriptor<T>(...)` when they have tenant-owned entities. The empty case is a tested code path returning an empty manifest + a README explaining the empty result.
- **Synchronous-only delivery for v1.** Do NOT scaffold the async/email path in this packet. The async path requires a queue substrate and a Communications-side email template — both deferred. The sync path is sufficient for v1 partition sizes.
- **Signed URL TTL is 7 days, configurable.** Default 7 days per D7. Configuration may override; the default is 7.
- **Rate limit is 24 hours per tenant, configurable.** Default 24 hours per D7. Configuration may override.
- **Audit emissions use the new pseudonymous-token factory.** `AuditEntry.CreatePseudonymous(...)` from packet 02. Never the legacy `string Actor` constructor.
- **Failure paths emit a Failed audit event.** Don't swallow the exception or skip the audit emission on storage failure.
- **`HoneyDrunk.Data.Abstractions` stays Abstractions-only.** New references to `HoneyDrunk.Auth.Abstractions` and `HoneyDrunk.Audit.Abstractions` are acceptable (both are Abstractions packages, invariant 1 preserved). No new HoneyDrunk runtime dependencies.
- **Records drop the `I`.** `TenantExportResult`, `TenantExportEntry`, `TenantExportManifest` are records. Interfaces keep `I`.
- **Invariant 27 — version bump every non-test `.csproj` in one commit.** No partial bumps.

## Labels
`feature`, `tier-2`, `core`, `adr-0050`, `wave-4`

## Agent Handoff

**Objective:** Implement the tenant-data export pipeline in `HoneyDrunk.Data`: contract surface in Abstractions, runtime that emits a ZIP with manifest + NDJSON + CSV + schema + README, uploads to Azure Blob, returns a 7-day signed URL, rate-limited per tenant per day, audited via `TenantDataExported`. Bump the solution to `0.7.0`.

**Target:** `HoneyDrunk.Data`, branch from `main`.

**Context:**
- Goal: Ship the export pipeline ADR-0050 D7 specifies. The customer-portal trigger and the async/email delivery path are deferred follow-ups; this packet ships the sync export contract + runtime.
- Feature: ADR-0050 Tenant Lifecycle rollout, Wave 4.
- ADRs: ADR-0050 D5/D6/D7 (primary), ADR-0026 (`TenantId` primitive), ADR-0008 (packet conventions).

**Acceptance Criteria:** As listed above.

**Dependencies:**
- `packet:03` — `HoneyDrunk.Auth` v0.6.0 ships `IIdentityMap` (used to resolve the tenant's `PseudoTenantToken`).

**Constraints:**
- **Tenant-scoped data only.** Exclude audit, telemetry, Stripe records. Test the exclusions.
- **Empty exportable-entity registry is a valid path.** No registered descriptors → empty manifest + explanatory README + valid signed URL.
- **Synchronous-only delivery for v1.** Don't scaffold the async/email path here.
- **Rate limit 1 per 24h per tenant; signed URL TTL 7 days; both configurable.**
- **Audit emissions use `AuditEntry.CreatePseudonymous` with pseudonymous tokens.** Resolve the tenant token via `IIdentityMap`.
- Records drop the `I`; interfaces keep it.
- Bump every non-test `.csproj` to `0.7.0` in one commit (invariant 27). This is the bumping packet for `HoneyDrunk.Data` in this initiative.

**Key Files:**
- `src/HoneyDrunk.Data.Abstractions/TenantExport/` (new folder with contracts)
- `src/HoneyDrunk.Data/TenantExport/` (new folder with implementations)
- DI extension
- Every non-test `.csproj` for the version bump
- Repo-level `CHANGELOG.md`; per-package CHANGELOGs; READMEs

**Contracts:**
- `ITenantDataExporter` (new interface) — `ExportAsync(TenantId, PseudoUserToken, CancellationToken)`.
- `TenantExportResult`, `TenantExportEntry`, `TenantExportManifest` (new records).
- `ITenantExportRateLimiter`, `TenantExportRateLimitException`.
- `ITenantExportableEntity` — descriptor for hosts to register tenant-scoped entities.
- Default runtime + in-memory rate limiter in `HoneyDrunk.Data`.

items.title: Research(ai-gateway): evaluate FrugalGPT model cascading for IELTS Task 1 and diagnostic grading to reduce inference costs

labels.name: ready-for-agent
labels.description: Đã đặc tả đủ, agent AFK làm được ngay

labels.name: P3
labels.description: When time allows, or waiting for a recorded trigger

milestone.title: Research and evaluations
milestone.description: Evaluations that end in an adopt-or-decline decision record. Not launch work: an issue here ships nothing until its evaluation is accepted and a follow-up issue is filed in the milestone that owns the change.

items.body:
## What to build

Evaluate the FrugalGPT model cascading strategy (Stanford University & Databricks paper: arXiv:2305.05176) within AIHUB's grading pipeline to route simple IELTS submissions (such as Task 1 report summaries or low-complexity diagnostic exercises) to lightweight, cost-effective models while reserving expensive frontier models for complex or borderline essays.

### Problem Context
Currently, all IELTS Writing submissions unconditionally dispatch to the same top-tier downstream foundation model:
1. **Uniform Cost for Unequal Complexity**: A simple IELTS Writing Task 1 submission (e.g. 150-word bar chart description with straightforward vocabulary) incurs the exact same token pricing and 8–15s end-to-end latency as an intricate 400-word Task 2 discursive essay.
2. **Deterministic Grading on Clear Bands**: Submissions with severe grammatical breakdowns (clear Band 4.5–5.0) or high-volume diagnostic trial runs do not require multi-billion parameter frontier reasoning to accurately identify errors and calculate band scores.
3. **Budget and Concurrency Pressure**: During exam peaks or school-wide test simulations, uniform top-tier dispatch saturates downstream TPM/RPM quotas and increases token expenditure unnecessarily.

### Architectural Solution: FrugalGPT Cascading Pipeline
- **Stage 1 (Lightweight / Distilled Scorer)**: Dispatches the prompt and rubric criteria to a fast, low-cost model or specialized distilled evaluator. The model returns estimated criteria band scores (TR/CC/LR/GRA) and an overall confidence score based on scoring entropy and rubric boundary variance.
- **Stage 2 (Escalation Gate & Confidence Evaluation)**:
  - If the confidence score meets or exceeds the defined threshold ($\tau$) and criteria variance is low, the Stage 1 result is finalized and returned immediately (latency dropped to ~1.5–2.5s, 80%+ token cost savings).
  - If the confidence score is below threshold, or if criteria conflict is detected (e.g. borderline Band 6.5 vs 7.0 where fine-grained human-like reasoning is essential), the submission cascades to Stage 3.
- **Stage 3 (Frontier Model Fallback)**: Dispatches the full grading prompt to the primary frontier model, incorporating prior stage hints where appropriate to refine evaluation.
- **Organization Policy & SLA Configuration**: Allows organizations to opt-in to strict frontier-only routing (e.g. for official certificate-grade examinations) versus cost-optimized cascading for practice and diagnostic sessions.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Architectural evaluation document referencing arXiv:2305.05176, defining the multi-stage cascade architecture, confidence scoring heuristics, and latency/cost trade-offs.
- [ ] Synthetic benchmark suite comparing scoring accuracy, criteria variance, token cost, and TTFT across a dataset of 200 IELTS Task 1 and Task 2 sample essays.
- [ ] Specification of fallback and escalation thresholds ($\tau$) ensuring grading accuracy matches or exceeds standalone frontier grading.
- [ ] Tenant-level configuration schema in `OrganizationIdentityConfiguration` permitting per-organization policy selection (e.g. `cascade_enabled: boolean`).
- [ ] `bun run verify` passes.

## Blocked by

None - can start immediately. Complements #1005, #1103, and #1549.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/55dbfced-d9b2-4e59-871d-31f3ba4aef3c)

# SPEC-023: Document Parser Module — Schema-Driven AI Extraction with Preview and Human-in-the-Loop Editing

## Overview

Add a new `document_parser` module to `@open-mercato/core` that provides schema-driven AI document extraction with multi-provider LLM consensus, PDF page preview, and human-in-the-loop result editing. The module turns uploaded documents (invoices, purchase orders, receipts, contracts, customs forms) into structured, validated data using predefined YAML schemas — with full support for custom schemas per tenant.

**Why this matters:** Every ERP system receives documents from external parties — vendor invoices, bank statements, shipping documents, purchase orders. Today these are manually read and re-keyed into the system. This module automates the extraction using LLM providers while keeping humans in the loop for verification and correction. The YAML-based schema system makes it extensible without code changes — a tenant can define a new document type schema and immediately start extracting structured data from it.

**Relationship to Financial Management Module (#260):** This module is designed as a foundational building block for the Financial Management Module. Extracted vendor invoices feed directly into Accounts Payable (AP invoice creation, three-way matching against POs). Extracted bank statements feed into bank reconciliation. The module is deliberately generic — it extracts structured data from any document type, and downstream modules consume that data.

**Relationship to InboxOps (#573):** Complementary to InboxOps which handles email-to-ERP proposals. Document Parser handles the attachment processing that InboxOps defers to Phase 2. The two modules can integrate: InboxOps receives an email with a PDF invoice attachment -> Document Parser extracts structured data -> InboxOps creates an AP invoice proposal with pre-filled fields.

## Architecture

### Core Flow

1. **Upload** — User uploads a document (PDF, image, DOCX) via drag-and-drop dialog or API. The file is stored via the existing `attachments` module.

2. **OCR** — Raw text is extracted from the document using Mistral OCR (or configurable provider). For image-based PDFs, OCR produces searchable text.

3. **Classification** — The `DocumentDetector` scores the text against all registered YAML schemas using weighted pattern matching. Each schema defines detection patterns (regex + weight), required patterns, negative patterns, and a minimum score threshold. The highest-scoring type above threshold wins.

4. **Parallel LLM Extraction** — The document text is sent to multiple LLM providers simultaneously (configurable: Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, Mistral). Each provider extracts structured data according to the Zod schema generated from the YAML definition. Providers run in parallel for speed.

5. **Consensus Engine** — Results from all providers are compared field-by-field. The consensus engine resolves disagreements using majority voting, confidence scoring, and format validation. Fields where providers disagree are flagged with low confidence. The engine produces a recommendation: `APPROVE` (high confidence across all fields) or `MANUAL_REVIEW` (disagreements detected).

6. **Result Storage** — Two copies are stored: `extractedData` (immutable audit trail of what LLMs returned) and `documentData` (editable working copy for user corrections). Key fields are also written to real indexed columns for fast search and filtering.

7. **Preview & Edit UI** — A detail panel shows the PDF page preview on the left and extracted data sections on the right. Users can edit any field. Sections are dynamically generated from the YAML schema — no UI code changes needed for custom document types.

### Schema-Driven Architecture

Document types are defined entirely in YAML files. Each schema specifies:

```yaml
schema:
  version: "1.0"
  name: "Vendor Invoice"
  documentType: "vendor_invoice"

detection:
  patterns:
    - regex: "invoice|faktura|rechnung"
      weight: 50
    - regex: "VAT|tax.?id|NIP"
      weight: 30
  requiredPatterns:
    - "invoice|faktura|rechnung"
  negativePatterns:
    - regex: "proforma|pro.?forma"
      weight: -20
  minScore: 40

fields:
  invoice_number:
    type: string
    required: true
    description: "Invoice number/identifier"
  invoice_date:
    type: date
    required: true
    description: "Date the invoice was issued"
  seller:
    type: object
    properties:
      name:
        type: string
        required: true
      tax_id:
        type: string
  line_items:
    type: array
    itemSchema:
      description:
        type: string
        required: true
      quantity:
        type: decimal
      gross_amount:
        type: decimal
        required: true
  currency:
    type: string
    required: true

normalization:
  rules:
    - path: "line_items.*.gross_amount"
      transform: decimal_2dp
    - path: "invoice_date"
      transform: iso_date
    - path: "currency"
      transform: uppercase
```

**Predefined schemas** ship with the module:
- Vendor Invoice
- Purchase Order
- Receipt / Proof of Payment
- Bank Statement
- Delivery Note
- Credit Memo

**Custom schemas** can be added per tenant via a settings UI or by placing YAML files in a configurable directory. The `SchemaRegistry` hot-loads them at runtime.

### Key Design Decisions

1. **YAML-first schema system** — Document types are data, not code. Adding a new type requires only a YAML file with detection patterns and field definitions. The system generates Zod schemas, JSON Schema (for structured output APIs), and extraction prompts automatically.

2. **Multi-provider consensus** — Running 2-3 LLM providers in parallel and voting on results dramatically reduces hallucination risk for critical fields (amounts, dates, identifiers). Single-provider mode is supported for cost-sensitive deployments.

3. **Dual data copies** — `extractedData` is the immutable audit trail (what the AI actually returned). `documentData` is the working copy users edit. This preserves provenance while allowing corrections.

4. **Real columns for key fields** — Document number, date, currency, seller, amount, and other frequently-filtered fields are stored as real indexed database columns, not just inside JSONB. This enables fast DynamicTable filtering and sorting.

5. **Schema-driven UI** — The detail panel sections (field groups, tables, nested objects) are generated from the YAML schema definition. Custom document types get a working UI automatically.

## Risks & Impact Review

#### LLM Provider Unavailability
- **Scenario**: One or more LLM providers (Mistral, Claude, Gemini) are down or rate-limited during extraction
- **Severity**: Medium
- **Affected area**: Document extraction pipeline, processing status stuck in `processing`
- **Mitigation**: Consensus engine works with 1+ providers; configurable timeout per provider (default 30s); pipeline marks document as `failed` with error details if all providers fail; user can re-trigger extraction later
- **Residual risk**: Single-provider extraction has lower confidence; acceptable for non-critical documents

#### OCR Quality on Scanned Documents
- **Scenario**: Poor scan quality leads to garbled OCR text, causing misclassification and extraction errors
- **Severity**: Medium
- **Affected area**: All downstream processing (classification, extraction, real column population)
- **Mitigation**: Confidence scores flag low-quality extractions; `consensusRecommendation: 'MANUAL_REVIEW'` triggers human review; raw_text preserved for debugging
- **Residual risk**: Some documents will require manual data entry; this is expected and the UI supports it

#### JSONB Data Growth
- **Scenario**: `extractedData`, `documentData`, `processingResult` columns grow large for documents with many line items or complex structures
- **Severity**: Low
- **Affected area**: Database storage, query performance on detail view loads
- **Mitigation**: Real columns used for list/filter queries (not JSONB); JSONB only loaded on single-document detail view; list queries select only real columns
- **Residual risk**: Storage costs grow linearly with document count; acceptable at current scale

#### Tenant Data Isolation
- **Scenario**: Cross-tenant data leak via document queries or shared schema registry cache
- **Severity**: Critical
- **Affected area**: All API endpoints, schema registry
- **Mitigation**: Every query filters by `tenantId` and `organizationId`; commands enforce scope; custom schemas are tenant-scoped; predefined schemas are shared but read-only (no tenant data in them)
- **Residual risk**: None — scope enforcement is mandatory in all code paths

#### Concurrent Extraction Requests
- **Scenario**: Multiple users trigger extraction on the same document simultaneously
- **Severity**: Low
- **Affected area**: Document data consistency, wasted LLM API spend
- **Mitigation**: `processingStatus` check before starting extraction (reject if already `processing`); last-write-wins for real columns (acceptable since extraction is idempotent)
- **Residual risk**: Brief race condition window between status check and update; acceptable as extraction produces deterministic results

#### Custom Schema Injection
- **Scenario**: Malicious YAML content in custom schemas causes regex DoS (ReDoS) or extraction prompt injection
- **Severity**: High
- **Affected area**: Schema registry, document detection, LLM extraction prompts
- **Mitigation**: YAML validation endpoint checks regex complexity before saving; extraction prompts are templated with schema fields, not raw YAML content; regex patterns run with timeout; schema YAML size limit enforced
- **Residual risk**: Novel regex patterns may still cause slowdowns; monitoring needed

#### Migration & Deployment
- **Scenario**: Adding new table `parsed_documents` with indexes on a production database
- **Severity**: Low
- **Affected area**: Database migration, deployment downtime
- **Mitigation**: New tables only (no altering existing tables); `CREATE TABLE` and `CREATE INDEX` are non-blocking; migration is additive and backward-compatible
- **Residual risk**: None — no existing data affected

#### API Cost Control
- **Scenario**: Bulk document upload triggers hundreds of parallel LLM extractions, causing unexpected API bills
- **Severity**: Medium
- **Affected area**: LLM provider costs, API rate limits
- **Mitigation**: Extraction is opt-in (toggle in upload dialog); batch uploads queue extractions rather than running all in parallel; configurable concurrency limit; per-tenant extraction budget can be added in future
- **Residual risk**: No hard spending cap in Phase 1; acceptable for initial deployment with manual monitoring

items.title: Make PostgreSQL 18 the sole hosted catalog and remove admin.sqlite

labels.name: area:hosted
labels.description: Hosted service, accounts, billing, and provisioning

labels.name: engineering
labels.description: Implementation, reliability, performance, and infrastructure work

items.body:
## Outcome

Use PostgreSQL 18 as the sole hosted catalog and control-state database. Remove hosted production's local DuckLake catalog files and `admin.sqlite`, leaving the filesystem responsible only for telemetry/Parquet data.

## Current evidence

- `ops/prod/compose.yaml` does not set `SIGIRO_CATALOG_URL`, so hosted production currently selects `StorageMode::LocalFile` and stores each project's metadata in `catalog.ducklake`.
- `src/storage.rs` selects the PostgreSQL-backed DuckLake catalog only when `SIGIRO_CATALOG_URL` is set and attaches it with a per-tenant metadata schema.
- `src/main.rs` unconditionally calls `admin::open_admin_db`.
- `src/admin.rs` creates `admin.sqlite` and stores `instance_status`.
- `src/alerts.rs` creates `alert_instances`, `alert_occurrences`, and `alert_outbox` in the same SQLite database.
- `docs/notes/architecture/ducklake-integration.md` documents `admin.sqlite` as a second administrative store beside either DuckLake catalog mode.

The hosted target already needs PostgreSQL for Better Auth and the shared catalog. Keeping SQLite creates a second persistence and backup path without an independent availability boundary.

## Target data model

One PostgreSQL 18 cluster contains separate databases and roles:

- `pipeline` — BenchApp;
- `sigiro` — DuckLake metadata plus Sigiro administrative and alert state;
- `sigiro_auth` — Better Auth.

Within `sigiro`:

- DuckLake keeps its tenant-specific metadata schemas;
- Sigiro-owned administrative tables live in an explicit application schema;
- instance status and alert outbox transitions retain their current atomicity and uniqueness constraints.

Filesystem layout:

```text
/var/lib/postgresql/18/main       PostgreSQL cluster
/var/lib/sigiro/telemetry/       durable tenant Parquet data
/var/cache/sigiro/duckdb/        rebuildable extension cache
```

Do not place telemetry or cache files inside PostgreSQL `PGDATA`.

## Migration

1. Add a PostgreSQL implementation for instance status and alert state using the existing SQL layer; do not duplicate query logic across SQLite and PostgreSQL in hosted mode.
2. Add a one-shot, idempotent migration that imports the current `admin.sqlite` rows and records a completion marker in PostgreSQL.
3. Add a verified DuckLake metadata/data migration from each local `catalog.ducklake` project into the PostgreSQL catalog while preserving tenant identity and local Parquet files.
4. Point hosted production at the PostgreSQL catalog with TLS and full server-certificate verification.
5. Move the persistent data root to `/var/lib/sigiro/telemetry` and the extension cache to `/var/cache/sigiro/duckdb`.
6. Refuse startup when hosted mode sees a partially migrated or incompatible catalog rather than silently creating empty state.
7. Remove `admin.sqlite` from the hosted backup contract after row-level migration verification; retain the original encrypted archive for rollback.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Hosted production sets and validates `SIGIRO_CATALOG_URL` for PostgreSQL 18.
- [ ] Every existing tenant/project is present in the PostgreSQL DuckLake catalog with matching table and metadata counts.
- [ ] Existing Parquet telemetry remains queryable after migration.
- [ ] `instance_status`, `alert_instances`, `alert_occurrences`, and `alert_outbox` are stored in PostgreSQL with equivalent constraints and transactional behavior.
- [ ] Hosted startup no longer creates or opens `admin.sqlite`.
- [ ] `/var/lib/sigiro/telemetry` contains durable telemetry only; `/var/cache/sigiro/duckdb` is safe to delete and rebuild.
- [ ] All PostgreSQL application connections use TLS with `verify-full`; non-TLS TCP is rejected.
- [ ] Migration is idempotent, fail-closed, and covered by an end-to-end test using copies of the real storage shapes.
- [ ] Backup and restore tests cover the PostgreSQL databases and telemetry directory together.
- [ ] Documentation names PostgreSQL as the only hosted catalog/control store and no longer describes `admin.sqlite` as hosted state.

## Compatibility boundary

Self-hosted zero-infrastructure local mode may retain its local DuckLake catalog. This issue removes the extra SQLite control store from the hosted PostgreSQL-backed mode; it does not make every self-hosted installation depend on PostgreSQL.

items.title: Fivetran lineage binds same-named tables to the first service in dbServiceNames
items.body:
### Connector

Fivetran

### Feature area

Lineage

### Describe the bug

When several services in `lineageInformation.dbServiceNames` hold a table with the same database, schema and name, the Fivetran connector attaches every connector's lineage to the first listed service.

`_resolve_table` in `pipeline/fivetran/metadata.py` loops over `dbServiceNames` in order and returns the first service where `<service>.<database or *>.<schema>.<table>` exists. It never uses which source the Fivetran connector actually reads from. Sharded or per-tenant estates, where several databases share one schema, are the common case.

In our instance six MySQL services hold the same `evo` schema, one per Fivetran connector. With all six in one agent's `dbServiceNames`, all six connectors' 273 table edges were attached to the first service. Nothing was logged and the run reported success.

### To Reproduce

1. Two database services, A and B, each with table `db.schema.t`.
2. Two Fivetran connectors, one syncing from A and one from B.
3. A Fivetran agent with `dbServiceNames: [A, B]`.
4. Both connectors' lineage originates from A.

### Expected behavior

The source service is chosen from the Fivetran connector's own source (for example its configured host, or its database/service type), or the ambiguity is reported and the edge skipped rather than bound to the first match.

Our workaround is one Fivetran agent per source service, each with a `pipelineFilterPattern` and only its own service in `dbServiceNames`.

### OS

Kubernetes (ingestion-base image)

### Python version

3.12

### OpenMetadata version

2.0.6

### OpenMetadata Ingestion package version

openmetadata-ingestion==2.0.1.0; same logic on main.

### Pre-submission checklist

- [x] I searched for duplicate issues.
- [x] I removed credentials, hostnames, emails, and other sensitive data from logs and config.

## Frontmatter

---

blueprint_sections: ["section-17-Module3", "section-XII-Layer7"]

acceptance:
  - System prompt architecture: locked compliance system prompt (signed by compliance officer, versioned in git under packages/compliance-rules/); client context pack (RAG top-k from client vault and scores); optional advisor notes; compliance guardrails (forbidden topics list, required disclaimer injection)
  - Compliance guardrails enforced in output: output classifier runs on every completion before delivery; blocks responses containing guarantee language, specific APR promises, exact approval claims; injects required CROA/FCRA disclaimers when credit topics detected
  - RAG retrieval: Pinecone per-tenant namespace populated from vault documents; embedding model (Claude or text-embedding-3-large); 512-token chunks with 64-token overlap; event-driven refresh on vault updates; nightly full rebuild job
  - Structured output mode: tool-use schema for non-conversational tasks (action plan generation, lender memo drafting, credit position summary); validated against Pydantic schema before delivery
  - Streaming SSE for chat surfaces: first token delivered within 600ms at p95 per spec section-13.1 SLO
  - Claude as primary model; OpenAI GPT-4 as fallback when Claude unavailable or ANTHROPIC_BUDGET_HARD_CAP approached; fallback transparent to user
  - Evaluation golden set: 50 representative prompt-response pairs covering all coaching scenarios; regression run on every prompt system change; any degradation blocks merge
  - Human-in-the-loop sampling: 1 percent of completions randomly sampled and queued for human review; review interface in admin console; results feed back into golden set
  - Citation-required mode for factual claims about lender criteria or credit thresholds; uncited factual claims blocked by guardrail
  - Conversation history stored in coaching schema (schema 7) with per-tenant namespace; history retrieved for context window packing
  - Token usage tracked per session per tenant per day; logged to analytics schema for cost monitoring per issue #139
---

## Details

This issue covers the Coaching LLM Stack implementation per spec section-12.5. Issue #124 covers the Module 3 AI Readiness Coaching System functional requirements (what the coaching system does for the user). This issue covers the LLM-specific implementation: the prompt architecture, compliance guardrails, RAG retrieval pipeline, structured output handling, evaluation framework, and human sampling loop.

The compliance guardrails are the most critical component. The coaching system operates near regulatory boundaries (CROA credit improvement guidance, FCRA credit dispute language, ECOA fair lending concerns). The guardrail system must prevent the LLM from generating content that creates legal risk for the platform. The locked compliance system prompt is signed by the compliance officer and any change requires compliance-officer-approved label per the bootstrap rider.

RAG retrieval: the coaching system is only as good as its context. The client's vault documents (bank statements, tax returns, formation docs) are chunked and indexed in Pinecone. The retrieval system must surface the most relevant chunks for the user's current question. The refresh pipeline must be event-driven (triggered by vault.document.processed event) to keep the index current.

Evaluation discipline: without a golden set regression, every prompt change is a blind deployment. The 50-pair golden set covers: assessment result explanation, action recommendation, credit dispute guidance, lender preparation advice, and general coaching questions. Degradation on any category blocks the change.

References: engineering-spec-v1.0.html section-12.5, section-3.3, section-3.2 (compliance guardrail integration)

labels.name: area:infra
labels.description: Terraform, Helm, GKE, CI/CD, secrets, cost

items.body:
As a team sharing a Lore installation, I want my data separated by enforced access rules and restorable on its own, so that another team can neither read it nor be restored over it.

<!-- lore-backlog-reconciled: 3971/full-review-v1 -->

## Backlog reconciliation

Reviewed against main at `3cb0d923c43d05e3ba03adb67b73c3acc61bce2d` using independent Codex review. Assessment: **partial**.

CNPG and backup infrastructure exist, but the pinned configuration still has one instance, 7d barman retention and a 30-day bucket lifecycle. Commented recovery bootstrap is not a restore runbook, executed drill or measured RTO/RPO, and does not establish tenant isolation.

### Remaining work

Document the deployment tenant boundary and decide per-tenant cluster versus RLS; implement/verify the chosen isolation, HA/retention alignment, recovery and per-team export runbooks, and an authorized timed restore drill.

### Evidence

- [infra/terraform/lore-db.tf:44–51](https://github.com/re-cinq/lore/blob/3cb0d923c43d05e3ba03adb67b73c3acc61bce2d/infra/terraform/lore-db.tf#L44-L51)
- [infra/terraform/lore-db.tf:88–96](https://github.com/re-cinq/lore/blob/3cb0d923c43d05e3ba03adb67b73c3acc61bce2d/infra/terraform/lore-db.tf#L88-L96)
- [infra/terraform/lore-db.tf:130–132](https://github.com/re-cinq/lore/blob/3cb0d923c43d05e3ba03adb67b73c3acc61bce2d/infra/terraform/lore-db.tf#L130-L132)
- [infra/terraform/lore-db.tf:152–167](https://github.com/re-cinq/lore/blob/3cb0d923c43d05e3ba03adb67b73c3acc61bce2d/infra/terraform/lore-db.tf#L152-L167)

Source review is not a claim of successful behavioral or production verification.

This assessment follows #3971 and PR #3972; it does not attribute all prior implementation to that change.

## Current acceptance criteria

- [ ] The tenant model and access isolation are explicit and enforced.
- [ ] CNPG has the agreed HA replica count and coherent recoverable retention.
- [ ] A timed restore and team export are demonstrated with measured RTO/RPO.

<details>
<summary>Original filing retained for scope, relationships, and audit history</summary>

### Schema-per-team is a retrieval partition, not tenant isolation (no RLS, one role); per-tenant recovery is whole-cluster PITR with no runbook or drill

asks about PostgreSQL-native RLS and restoring an individual tenant database. In code, a 'tenant' is a whole Lore deployment (one org). Team schemas only split the vector corpus, and one DB role reads all of them. Tasks, agent transcripts, memory and audit data share one schema per concern, with no RLS anywhere. Recovery: WAL archiving and daily base backups give cluster-level point-in-time recovery for 7 days on a single-instance cluster. There is no documented or tested restore procedure. Restoring one team or tenant means restoring the whole cluster to a side instance and dumping one schema.

**Evidence**
- `scripts/infra/setup-db.sh:97-144 (team schemas hold only <team>.chunks; all owned and read by the single `lore` role)`
- `apps/lore-api/src/transport/routes/context/search-context.ts:67-80 (team miss falls back to org_shared), chunk-schema-readers.ts:49 (browser unions every team schema)`
- `pipeline.*, memory.*, lore.* are org-wide schemas (setup-pipeline-schema.sh, setup-memory-schema.sh, setup-repos-schema.sh); grep finds no ROW LEVEL SECURITY / CREATE POLICY anywhere`
- `infra/terraform/lore-db.tf:131 (instances = 1), :177-183 (barman WAL archiver = PITR capable), :224-244 (daily base backup), :95 (7d retention) vs :44-51 (30d bucket lifecycle), :152-167 (restore only as a commented-out bootstrap block)`
- `runbooks/ holds only dark-factory-rollback.md and station-consolidation-cutover.md (no restore runbook)`

**Proposed change**
Before the call: write runbooks/db-restore.md (a CNPG recovery Cluster from the barman ObjectStore with a targetTime, then pg_dump -n <schema> for a partial restore). Run a timed restore drill and record the RTO and RPO. State the tenancy model honestly: deployment per tenant. Architecture options to bring: (a) a CNPG Cluster per tenant, which makes per-tenant PITR native and fits the existing terraform; (b) a shared DB with RLS on the memory, pipeline and lore tables keyed by repo or team, a per-request `SET app.tenant`, and non-owner app roles. Option (b) is a large migration across 32 models and needs an ADR. Also: move to instances >= 2 and align the 7d/30d retention.


Also: the CloudNativePG cluster runs `instances = 1` with 7-day backup retention against a 30-day bucket lifecycle (`infra/terraform/lore-db.tf`), and restore exists only as a commented-out `bootstrap.recovery` block. A per-tenant restore runbook and a rehearsal are missing.


_Found in a codebase audit on 2026-10-01 (main @ 0fabcf525); each point was checked against the code by a second reviewer._

</details>

items.title: Design spec: feeds, durable push ingestion (pluggable append-only storage) as a layer on top of runs

labels.name: feature
labels.description: Brand-new capability (e.g. new connector, new transform)

labels.name: tier-2
labels.description: Important priority — significant improvement or popular request

labels.name: needs-design
labels.description: Open design questions must be resolved before implementation; do not pick up

milestone.title: Phase 3: SaaS via Template Hub
milestone.description: Exit: broad SaaS coverage through maintained REST/GraphQL templates and Singer targets, without a native crate per API.

items.body:
> **Design spec. Labelled `needs-design`: don't build until every point in "Open decisions" (§15) has a recorded decision.**
> Philosophy (the why, red lines, litmus test) is in the **first comment**; read it before changing anything here.
> Must land first: #1032 (webhook source acknowledges before the sink commits; same ack-after-commit principle the feed cursor relies on).
> Picking this up months later? Start with **"Re-validate first"** at the end.

## Summary
A **feed** is a named, durable, **append-only** log that senders push events into over HTTP. `faucet serve` stores each event in a **pluggable feed store** (SQLite, PostgreSQL, object storage, later brokers and others) and acknowledges only after it is durable. **Consumers** bind a feed to an ordinary pipeline with a **flush policy**. When the policy fires, the feed layer submits a **normal run** whose source (`type: feed`) reads a fixed range of the log, and it advances the consumer's cursor **only after the run's sink commits**.

Feeds are a **layer on top of runs**: they never write to sinks themselves, so transforms, governance, delivery guarantees, DLQ, audit, tenants and metering all come from the existing run path. With no feed configured (or the `feeds` feature off), faucet behaves exactly as today.

```yaml
kind: feed
name: jira-issues
ingest:
  auth: { tokens: managed, signature: { header: X-Hub-Signature-256, secret: "${secret:vault:feeds/jira#hmac}", prefix: "sha256=" } }
  dedupe: { header: X-Atlassian-Webhook-Identifier, window: 24h }
retention: { max_age: 7d, undelivered: { max_age: 30d, max_bytes: 50GiB, on_exceeded: refuse } }
consumers:
  - name: to-iceberg
    pipeline: ./pipelines/jira_to_iceberg.yaml      # source: {type: feed}; sink: iceberg
    flush: { max_events: 5000, max_bytes: 64MiB, max_age: 60s }
```
Senders get `https://<serve>/v1/feeds/jira-issues/events` plus a write-only token or HMAC secret. That's the whole setup.

---

## Design discussion history (chronological)
1. **2026-11-01, discussion #1025:** a user asks for a permanently running webhook endpoint that ingests SaaS events (Jira, GitHub, Stripe, …) into Iceberg without losing events across restarts, comparing it with a streaming database's one-line webhook table. They note that `source-webhook` is a bounded in-memory window and that serve triggers can't pass the body on as records.
2. **2026-11-02, analysis:**
   - The diagnosis is correct. Worse: the webhook source acknowledges `200` before the sink commits, which led to bug #1032.
   - Options compared: a forever-running source (rejected: it fights the bounded-run model), trigger body as data (one run per event harms lake sinks), or an external queue (heavy for simple senders).
   - Proposed instead: a **durable inbox in serve plus micro-batched runs**.
   - Reply posted; the user answered with sizing:
     - SaaS/internal webhooks: 500 to tens of thousands/day;
     - Python analytics apps: up to 100k+/day;
     - a high-volume log bridge: hundreds of GB/day, judged out of scope;
     - file uploads: routed through object storage + `object_arrival`;
     - a single serve instance, about one minute of latency, HMAC for an internal Service Desk.
   - They offered to test a prototype.
3. **2026-11-02, which sources need it:** only `webhook` needs the full design (faucet is the server and senders don't keep data). `nats` (core subjects), `websocket` (live feeds) and `grpc` (non-resumable streams) need the always-on, durable half later, through ingress adapters. Every other source has upstream retention and is safe with bounded runs.
4. **2026-11-02, streaming-vertical exploration:** continuous runs made of checkpointed epochs, with replayable sources first and the durable inbox as the buffer for non-replayable ones. Feeds are the first concrete step; a continuous mode can later replace micro-runs under the same feed layer.
5. **2026-11-03, "channels" idea → named feed:** the owner proposed a first-class concept that keeps taking data, registers it durably, and is picked up by micro-runs. It was compared with a managed delivery-stream service that buffers by size/interval and delivers to sinks. The name **feed** was chosen ("channel" is already used for template channels and notify channels).
6. **2026-11-03, open source:** the whole feature is open source, including multi-tenant, quota, metering and cluster behaviour, consistent with how `faucet serve` already ships tenants, budgets, usage and cluster mode.
7. **2026-11-03, design thought through locally:** pluggable append-only storage, topologies (laptop / single node / Kubernetes / HA / multi-tenant), the safe-watermark invariant, and 22+ edge cases. Then **retention**: 7-day replay retention for delivered events, plus a separate 30-day / 50 GiB hard cap for undelivered events that refuses new events instead of deleting silently. Owner confirmed 7 days.

## Current state (verified on `main`, 2026-11-03)
| Fact | Where |
|---|---|
| `webhook` source: bounded receive window (`timeout_secs` / `max_payloads` / `max_buffered_bytes`), in-memory buffer, HMAC signature verification, constant-time token check; acknowledges `200` on buffering (#1032) | `crates/source/webhook/src/{stream.rs,config.rs}`, README |
| Serve triggers: `webhook`, `object_arrival`, `queue_depth`, `schedule`, with a shared watcher, enqueue + idempotency, health and metrics. `${trigger.body}` is a substitution string only, never records | `cli/src/serve/triggers/` (`watcher.rs`, `enqueue.rs`, `context.rs`, …) |
| Cluster mode: a claim loop pulls `Pending` runs from the shared SQL history DB; member leases and heartbeats; pools (#957) | `cli/src/serve/cluster.rs`, `cli/src/serve/server.rs`, `--pool` |
| RBAC: a closed `Permission` enum (`RunRead`, `RunWrite`, `TriggerFire`, `UsageRead`, `TenantAdmin`, …), with unmapped `/v1` routes falling to admin | `cli/src/serve/rbac.rs` |
| Per-tenant usage metering table `faucet_usage` | `cli/src/serve/history/sql.rs`, `overview.rs` |
| Per-run budgets (`max_records`, `max_bytes`); no ingest-rate quotas | `crates/core/src/budget.rs` |
| Ack-after-commit for message sources (`MessageConsumer::ack` / `ack_pending`), commit tokens (`CommitTokenDriver`) | `crates/core/src/driver/message.rs`, `crates/core/src/driver/sink.rs` |
| Runtime entry point for every serve operation (`Principal` → trust → policy → budget → tenant → governance → execution); a scan test forbids bypassing it | `cli/src/runtime/` |
| Helm chart: Deployment, HPA, PDB, Ingress, PVC, ServiceMonitor | `deploy/helm/faucet-stream/templates/` |

---
Origin: discussion https://github.com/orgs/faucet-hq/discussions/1025 (long-running webhook ingestion), the follow-up with real volumes, and the design conversation of 2026-11-02/03.
Open-source feature of `faucet serve`.

---

## 1. One-paragraph summary
A **feed** is a named, durable, **append-only** log of events that senders push into over HTTP (and later other ingress protocols). `faucet serve` accepts each event, stores it durably in a **pluggable feed store** (DB, object storage, local segment files, an existing broker, …), and only then acknowledges it. **Consumers** bind a feed to an ordinary faucet pipeline with a **flush policy**. When the policy fires, the feed layer **enqueues a normal run** whose source is `type: feed`, reading a fixed range of the log, and advances the consumer's **cursor only after that run's sink commits**. Feeds never move data to sinks themselves: all transformation, governance, delivery guarantees, DLQ and audit come from runs. Turning feeds off, or never configuring one, leaves faucet exactly as it is today.

## 2. Goals
1. **No event loss after acknowledgement:** ack = durably stored in the feed store.
2. **Configuration only:** a sender gets a URL plus a token/secret; no queue or custom receiver to deploy.
3. **A layer, not a fork:** feeds use only existing public machinery (runtime submission, runs, cluster claim loop, leases, StateStore/commit tokens, governance, RBAC, tenants, usage). No change to `Source`/`Sink` traits; existing pipelines are unaffected.
4. **Pluggable storage** behind one append-only log interface; operators choose per feed.
5. **Works on every topology:** laptop, single VM, Kubernetes with many replicas, HA/multi-AZ, multi-tenant.
6. **Micro-batched delivery:** a run per flush (records/bytes/age), never per event (protects lake sinks from small commits).
7. **Fan-out and replay:** several consumers per feed with independent cursors; replay by resetting a cursor within retention.
8. **Observable:** depth, lag, oldest-unconsumed age, ingest rate, rejects, stalled consumers.

## 3. Non-goals (v1)
- Being a message broker: no partitions or consumer-group rebalancing in v1, no cross-region replication, no pub/sub semantics beyond cursors.
- Sub-second end-to-end latency (micro-runs aim at seconds to a minute; the later continuous-run/epoch mode covers lower latency under the same feed layer).
- High-volume log/metrics shipping (hundreds of GB/day, syslog/OTLP firehoses): Vector/Kafka territory.
- Bulk file upload (route through object storage + the `object_arrival` trigger).
- Browser/mobile beacons with public write keys (needs abuse protection; v2).

---

## 4. Architecture

```
 senders ──HTTP POST──▶ [ingest endpoint]──verify/limit──▶ FeedStore.append ──▶ 202 (after durable)
                          (serve route, any replica)                │
                                                                     ▼
                                                           append-only log per feed
                                                           seq 1,2,3,…  (+ retention)
                                                                     │
  feed trigger (scheduler, one owner per consumer via lease) ── watches head/cursor/age
         │ flush policy met
         ▼
  runtime.submit(run: pipeline + source {type: feed, feed, consumer, range [from, to)})
         │  (normal run: Principal → trust → policy → budget → tenant → governance → execution)
         ▼
  cluster claim loop / local executor runs it → transforms → governed sink write (commit token = feed:consumer:from-to)
         │ run succeeded (sink committed)
         ▼
  FeedStore.commit_cursor(consumer, expected=from, new=to)   ← CAS; only now is the batch "delivered"
```

| Component | Where | Reuses |
|---|---|---|
| `FeedStore` trait + backends | new crate `faucet-feed-store` (+ one crate or feature per backend) | `CallContext`, `faucet_core::http`, fidelity |
| Ingest routes | `cli/src/serve/feeds/ingest.rs` | serve router, body limits, auth middleware, RBAC (new permissions), tenants, audit, metrics |
| Feed registry (definitions, consumers, tokens) | history DB tables `faucet_feed*` (or a `kind: feed` YAML doc loaded like triggers) | history migrations, reload |
| Feed scheduler | **a new trigger kind `feed`** in `cli/src/serve/triggers/` | trigger watcher, enqueue + idempotency, health, metrics |
| `feed` source connector | `crates/source/feed` (a family driver, MessageConsumer-shaped: receive range / ack) | ack-after-commit (#1032 mechanism), commit tokens, `DESCRIPTOR`, conformance |

| CLI | `faucet feed create/list/push/tail/stats/cursor/replay/delete` | CLI contract (#1029) |
| Console | Feeds page (depth, lag, consumers, recent rejects) | `serve-ui` (mockups first, per CLAUDE.md) |

### Pluggability / non-interference rules
- Cargo feature `feeds` (in `full`, per the "full means every feature" rule) plus per-backend features. Without the feature: no routes, no tables, no tasks.
- With the feature but no feeds defined: routes return 404, no background work, migrations create empty tables only.
- Feeds call runs **only through `faucet_cli::runtime`** with a `Principal`, like triggers and MCP (the existing scan test forbids calling `run_expanded`/`load_submission*` directly).
- The `feed` source is an ordinary connector: it works in `faucet run` too (see §7), and it declares capabilities via `DESCRIPTOR`.
- Nothing in governance, delivery, state or other connectors changes.

## 5. Data model

### Feed (definition)
```yaml
kind: feed
name: jira-issues
tenant: acme                     # optional; tenant-scoped feeds live under /v1/tenants/{t}/feeds
store: { type: postgres, config: { url: "${secret:...}" } }   # or default store from serve config
ingest:
  auth:
    tokens: managed              # write-only tokens issued via API, stored hashed
    signature:                   # optional HMAC verifier (moved from the webhook source into core)
      header: X-Hub-Signature-256
      secret: "${secret:vault:feeds/jira#hmac}"
      algorithm: sha256
      prefix: "sha256="
      timestamp_header: null
  accept: [application/json, application/x-ndjson, application/x-www-form-urlencoded, text/plain]
  max_event_bytes: 1048576
  max_request_bytes: 10485760
  dedupe: { header: X-Atlassian-Webhook-Identifier, window: 24h }   # or body JSONPath
  rate_limit: { events_per_sec: 200, burst: 1000 }
retention:
  max_age: 7d                 # replay window for DELIVERED events (0 = delete as soon as every consumer has committed)
  max_bytes: null             # optional size cap for delivered data
  undelivered:
    max_age: 30d              # hard cap for events some active consumer hasn't committed
    max_bytes: 50GiB
    on_exceeded: refuse       # refuse (503 + Retry-After, default) | drop_oldest (writes a visible gap marker)
  warn_at: [0.5, 0.8]         # alert thresholds against the undelivered caps
consumers:
  - name: to-iceberg
    pipeline: ./pipelines/jira_to_iceberg.yaml   # or template: owner/name@version + params
    flush: { max_events: 5000, max_bytes: 64MiB, max_age: 60s, min_interval: 10s }
    max_batch: { events: 50000, bytes: 256MiB }  # cap per run (catch-up happens in chunks)
    start: earliest                              # earliest | latest | seq:N | time:RFC3339
    on_failure: { retries: 5, backoff: exponential, then: stall }   # stall | dlq_and_skip
```

### Event envelope (stored per event)
| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| `seq` | monotonic per feed (per partition later); **assigned by the store**, never by wall clock |
| `id` | ULID (returned to the sender) |
| `received_at` | ingest node clock (informational) |
| `dedupe_key` | from header/body, optional |
| `content_type`, `encoding` | raw body kept; decoding happens in the `feed` source (JSON / NDJSON split / form / text / bytes→base64) |
| `headers` | allow-listed subset only (never `Authorization`, cookies) |
| `payload` | bytes (optionally zstd-compressed in segment backends; optionally sealed with the tenant vault key) |
| `size` | for quotas/metering |

NDJSON / JSON-array requests become **multiple events** in one atomic append (all-or-nothing per request; per-item results are a v2 option).

### Consumer cursor
`(feed, consumer) → committed_seq`, plus `in_flight: {from, to, run_id, lease}`, stored transactionally with the feed store when the backend supports transactions, otherwise in the history DB with CAS.
