## 6. Storage backends (all append-only)

### The `FeedStore` interface (sketch)
```rust
trait FeedStore: Send + Sync {
    async fn append(&self, feed: &FeedId, events: Vec<NewEvent>) -> Result<AppendAck>;       // durable before Ok
    async fn read(&self, feed: &FeedId, from: Seq, to_max: Seq, limit: Limits) -> Result<Batch>; // [from, to)
    async fn head(&self, feed: &FeedId) -> Result<Head>;                // safe-to-read high watermark + stats
    async fn commit_cursor(&self, c: &ConsumerId, expected: Seq, new: Seq) -> Result<()>; // CAS
    async fn trim(&self, feed: &FeedId, below: Seq) -> Result<TrimStats>;  // retention
    fn capabilities(&self) -> StoreCaps;  // cluster_safe, transactional_cursor, max_event_bytes, ordering
}
```
The key invariant is the **safe-to-read watermark**: `head()` returns the highest `seq` such that **no event with a lower seq can still appear**. Readers never read past it. This is what prevents the classic "skipped event" bug (see edge case E1).

### Backend catalogue
| Backend | Cluster-safe | Durability on ack | Throughput (rough) | Ordering / watermark technique | Retention cost | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SQLite** (WAL) | no (single node) | fsync on commit | low–medium | single writer → seq = rowid; watermark = max committed | `DELETE` + incremental vacuum | laptop, dev, small single node |
| **Local segment files** (append-only log + index, fsync) | no | fsync per group commit | high | single writer per feed | delete whole segments | single node, high volume, no DB |
| **PostgreSQL** | yes | commit (sync replication if HA) | medium | seq from a sequence **+ commit-order watermark** (see E1: snapshot `xmin` / single append-lock per feed / `pg_current_snapshot()`); time-partitioned table | **drop partitions** (cheap) | Kubernetes / clustered serve (history DB already Postgres) |
| **MySQL / MariaDB** | yes | commit | medium | per-feed row lock for seq allocation; watermark = max committed | partitions | shops standardized on MySQL |
| **Object storage** (S3 / GCS / Azure / MinIO): immutable **segment objects** + manifest | yes | segment PUT complete (+ conditional-write manifest update) | high, latency = group window | manifest is the ordering authority; conditional writes (`If-None-Match` / generation preconditions) make manifest commits atomic | lifecycle rules / delete old segments | large volume, cheap long retention, multi-tenant deployments |
| **Hybrid: DB index + object-storage payloads** | yes | both writes done | high | DB holds seq/index/cursor; objects hold bodies (large events spill here) | DB partitions + lifecycle | big events (MB), cheap storage with fast index |
| **Bring-your-own broker**: Kafka/Redpanda, NATS JetStream, Redis Streams, Kinesis, Pub/Sub | yes | broker ack (acks=all / JetStream ack / XADD) | very high | broker offsets = seq; cursor = consumer offset/committed id | broker retention | teams that already run a broker but want the HTTP front door + faucet consumers |
| **Lake table** (Iceberg/Delta as the log) | yes | table commit | medium (commit cost) | snapshot order; must buffer → ack latency = commit interval | expire snapshots | "raw landing zone that is also queryable"; better as a **cold tier** than as the hot log |
| **DynamoDB / key-value** | yes | write ack | high | per-feed bucket + sort key; seq via atomic counter (hot key risk) | TTL | AWS-native serverless setups |

**Tiering (v2):** hot backend (Postgres / local / broker) → compacted **Parquet segments in object storage** after N hours. Consumers read transparently across tiers; long retention gets cheap.

**Recommendation for v1:** SQLite (local), Postgres (cluster), object-storage segments (scale). v2: hybrid, local segment files, BYO broker (Kafka, JetStream, Redis Streams), tiering. Experimental later: lake-table, DynamoDB.

**Capability checks at load:** `serve --cluster` with a non-cluster-safe store (SQLite, local segments) is **refused at startup** with a clear error, so a misconfiguration can't silently split feeds across replicas.

## 7. Topologies

### 7.1 Laptop / local
- `faucet serve` (no cluster) + SQLite or local-segment store under a data dir (not cwd/tmp; 0700 dir, 0600 files).
- **Without a server:** ingest needs a long-lived endpoint, so **ingest requires `faucet serve`**. But the store is a plain backend, so:
  - `faucet feed push <feed> < events.ndjson` appends directly (operator-side tool, uses store credentials, for tests/backfills);
  - `faucet run pipeline.yaml` with `source: {type: feed, feed: x, consumer: y}` drains it once (reads from cursor to the watermark at start, commits cursor after sink). Useful for dev, cron-only setups and replays;
  - a lock/lease on the consumer prevents a CLI drain and a serve-scheduled run from consuming the same range concurrently.

### 7.2 Single node production (VM / systemd / one container)
- serve + Postgres (recommended) or SQLite/local segments on a persistent volume + backups.
- Restart: in-flight runs are re-scheduled from the committed cursor; ingest unavailable during restart (senders retry; document `Retry-After` behaviour and sender retry policies).

### 7.3 Kubernetes, multiple replicas
- **Ingest is stateless:** any replica accepts any feed's events and appends to the shared store (Postgres or object storage). Readiness probe fails while draining so the Service stops routing; preStop finishes in-flight appends.
- **Scheduling:** each consumer has **one owner** at a time, a lease in the history DB (existing lease/member machinery). The owner evaluates flush policy and enqueues runs; on owner loss another replica takes over after lease expiry (no double runs: enqueue is idempotent on `feed:consumer:from-to`).
- **Execution:** runs go through the existing **cluster claim loop** (`Pending` runs in the shared history DB) and **pools** (#957), so feed runs can be routed to a worker pool sized for them.
- **Roles (new, optional):** `faucet serve --role ingest|worker|all` so ingest pods (many, small, HPA on request rate) scale separately from worker pods (fewer, bigger, HPA on queue depth). `all` stays the default.
- **Helm:** values for feed store, ingest Service/Ingress (separate host/path so feeds can be public while the API stays private), NetworkPolicy, PDB, HPA per role, object-storage credentials via IRSA/Workload Identity.

### 7.4 HA / multi-AZ
- Durability = the store's durability: Postgres with synchronous replica (or managed multi-AZ), object storage (regional). Ack only after the store's durable commit.
- Ingest replicas spread across zones; leases survive zone loss (history DB HA).
- **Multi-region:** v1 = independent feeds per region (active/active ingestion, no global ordering); a global feed is out of scope.

### 7.5 Multi-tenant (serve tenants)
- Tenant-scoped feeds: `/v1/tenants/{t}/feeds/{f}/events`; tokens bound to tenant + feed.
- Per-tenant quotas: events/s, bytes/day, storage bytes, number of feeds; enforced at ingest (`429` / `503`).
- Usage metering into `faucet_usage` (events, bytes ingested, bytes stored·hours), the same table the console/overview reads.
- Storage isolation: per-tenant prefix (object storage) / per-tenant schema or row filter (DB); optional per-tenant payload sealing with the tenant vault key.

## 8. Ingest endpoint details
- `POST /v1/feeds/{feed}/events` (+ tenant form). Body: single event, NDJSON, or JSON array (configurable).
- **Auth (feed-scoped, write-only):** feed tokens (hashed, multiple active, rotation, expiry), optional HMAC verifier (generic: header, algorithm, encoding, prefix, timestamp header, tolerance), optional IP allow-list. Feed tokens grant **nothing else**: no read, no run, no admin. **Never** accept serve operator/admin tokens for ingest by default.
- **URL tokens:** some senders can only configure a URL. Allow `?token=` per feed **opt-in only**, redact it in every log/metric/audit line, warn in the console.
- **Limits:** request size, event size, JSON depth, decompression cap for `Content-Encoding: gzip`, rate limit per token/feed/tenant, concurrent connections, slow-request timeouts.
- **Responses:** `202 {ids, first_seq, last_seq}` only after durable append; `400` malformed, `401/403` auth, `409` duplicate (or `202` with `duplicate: true`, configurable since senders differ), `413` too large, `415` content type, `429` rate (with `Retry-After`), `503` store unavailable / feed full (`Retry-After`).
- **Group commit:** concurrent requests to the same feed are batched into one store append within a few ms (throughput) while every request is still acked only after its own events are durable.
- **Dedupe:** by header or body path within a window (store-side unique index or dedupe table), so sender retries don't duplicate.
- **CORS:** off; browser ingestion is v2.

---

## 9. Consumption details
- Flush policy fires when any of `max_events`, `max_bytes`, `max_age` (age of oldest unconsumed event) is reached and `min_interval` has passed; `max_batch` caps one run; backlog drains in consecutive runs.
- The enqueued run carries a **fixed range** `[from, to)` (to ≤ safe watermark). A retry of the same run reads the **same** range, so the sink commit token `feed:consumer:from-to` makes reruns idempotent (exactly-once for sinks with commit tokens; at-least-once otherwise, documented).
- **At most one in-flight run per consumer** (lease + CAS on cursor).
- Run success → `commit_cursor(expected=from, new=to)`. Run failure → cursor unchanged; retry with backoff; after N failures → `stall` (alert, console shows the failing range) or `dlq_and_skip` (move the range's raw events to the DLQ, advance, audit-log it).
- Record-level bad data uses the **existing per-record DLQ**; whole-run failures (sink down, config error) use the retry/stall policy.
- **Replay:** reset a cursor (admin, audited, change-request capable) to `seq`/time within retention, or create a new consumer with `start: time:...`.
- **Config changes:** a run always uses the consumer's current pipeline config; replays re-process with the current config (documented).
- **Ordering:** events reach the sink in `seq` order within a run and runs are sequential per consumer. Event-time order is not guaranteed (senders reorder) → recommend key + updated-at upserts.

## 10. Edge and corner cases (checklist for the spec and tests)
| # | Case | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | **Skipped events from out-of-order commits** (two appends get seq 10 and 11; 11 commits first; a reader at cursor 9 reads 11, commits cursor 11, then 10 commits → lost forever) | Readers stop at the **safe watermark**: single append lock per feed (simple, limits throughput), or commit-order watermark (Postgres: track in-flight appenders / snapshot `xmin`), or manifest-ordered segments (object storage). Conformance test with forced commit reordering |
| E2 | Run succeeded, crash before cursor commit | Rerun same range; commit token dedupes (exactly-once sinks) or duplicates (at-least-once sinks, documented) |
| E3 | Cursor commit CAS conflict | Means two owners: lease bug or manual reset race → abort, alert, never move backwards silently |
| E4 | Sender retries after a timeout although the append succeeded | Dedupe key; else duplicate is stored (at-least-once ingest) |
| E5 | Store down | Ingest `503 + Retry-After`; scheduler pauses; runs fail fast and retry |
| E6 | Undelivered data reaches its hard cap (a consumer stalled, e.g. sink down over a weekend) | `undelivered.on_exceeded: refuse` (default, no silent loss) → ingest `503 + Retry-After`; `drop_oldest` deletes the oldest undelivered events and **records a gap marker** the consumer sees and reports. Alerts at `warn_at` thresholds before either happens |
| E6a | Retention vs delivery | An event is deletable only when **older than `max_age` AND every active consumer has committed past it**. Deleted consumers never block; paused consumers block (with a warning) and count toward the undelivered cap |
| E6b | Retention clock and granularity | Age is measured from the store's `received_at` (never sender/event time); deletion runs in chunks (partition drop / whole segments / batched deletes), so "7d" means ≥7d and removed within ~1h after |
| E6c | Object-storage lifecycle rules | Not the retention mechanism (they ignore cursors); trimming is explicit. A bucket lifecycle rule is only a backstop set **longer** than `undelivered.max_age` |
| E7 | Consumer added with `start: earliest` after data was trimmed | Starts at the oldest retained seq, records a gap, warns; console/CLI show "replayable from …" |
| E8 | Poison batch (whole run crashes on it) | retries → stall or `dlq_and_skip` per policy; never loop forever silently |
| E9 | Event larger than limits | `413`; or spill to object storage with a pointer (hybrid backend) |
| E10 | Partially invalid batch request | all-or-nothing `400` with item errors (v1) |
| E11 | Clock skew between replicas | ordering never depends on clocks; `received_at` informational |
| E12 | Owner replica dies mid-run | lease expiry → new owner; the claimed run is handled by existing cluster fencing; enqueue idempotency prevents duplicates |
| E13 | Rolling upgrade with a store schema/segment format change | versioned migrations; readers support N and N-1 formats |
| E14 | Feed deleted / tenant deleted | soft delete → stop ingest, finish/cancel consumers, purge after retention; tenant delete purges feeds, tokens, cursors |
| E15 | Token leaked | rotate (multiple active tokens), per-token rate limits, audit of token use |
| E16 | Huge backlog after a long outage | `max_batch` chunks; optional `catch_up_parallelism` (v2, needs partitions) |
| E17 | Non-deterministic transforms on replay (`now()`, UUIDs) | fine with commit tokens; document |
| E18 | Personal data in payloads | retention limits, optional sealing, masking in the pipeline, data-subject deletion = trim by key (v2, hard on append-only stores; document) |
| E19 | Mixed content types in one feed | stored raw with content type; source decodes per event; undecodable → DLQ |
| E20 | Very low traffic | `max_age` guarantees delivery latency; no runs when empty |
| E21 | CLI drain and serve scheduler both active | consumer lease shared by both paths |
| E22 | Backups/restore of the store | restored cursors may be ahead of restored data (or behind) → validate on start, refuse to move cursor past head, report |

## 11. Security (feeds are an internet-facing ingest surface)
- The ingest listener enforces a Host/Origin allow-list and accepts only the configured content types (no cross-site simple requests).
- Separate listener/host for feeds is recommended so the control API can stay private.
- Write-only feed tokens + HMAC, constant-time compare, hashed storage, rotation, expiry, audit.
- Strict limits (size, depth, decompression, rate, connections, timeouts).
- Data at rest: store files 0600 / dirs 0700, DB/object-storage encryption, optional vault sealing.
- Never log payloads by default; redact tokens anywhere they could appear (including URL tokens).
- Threat-model and STRIDE rows for feeds in `docs/architecture/security.md`.

## 12. Observability
Metrics per feed/consumer/tenant: ingest requests by status, events and bytes in, append latency, store errors, depth (head − min cursor), lag (head − cursor), oldest unconsumed age, runs per consumer, run outcome, stalled consumers, retention trims and gaps, dedupe hits. Console Feeds page; alerts (lag > SLA, stalled, near full). Lineage: feed as a dataset (`feed://tenant/name`) upstream of the consumer pipeline.

2. **Phase 1:** feed definitions, ingest route (tokens, HMAC, limits, dedupe, group commit), `feed` source, `feed` trigger (flush policy, leases, ranges, cursor CAS), CLI `faucet feed`, metrics, docs, Helm values. Single node + cluster on Postgres.

## 15. Open decisions
1. Feed definitions: YAML docs loaded like triggers, API/DB-managed objects, or both (recommend both: YAML for GitOps, API for the console and automation).
2. Watermark technique per backend (single append lock first, commit-order watermark later?).
3. Duplicate response: `409` vs `202 duplicate:true`.
4. ~~Retention defaults~~ **Decided 2026-11-03: 7 days** replay retention for delivered events (covers a weekend outage plus time to notice; matches common broker defaults; cheap at expected volumes) and a **30-day / 50 GiB** hard cap for undelivered events with `on_exceeded: refuse`. Alternatives considered: 1 day (Firehose/Kinesis-like, less personal data at rest, but no replay window after a weekend outage). Server-wide default + per-feed override + optional per-tenant maximum (per-tenant retention tiers).
5. Default store when none is configured: the history DB backend (SQLite/Postgres) vs a dedicated data dir.
6. Roles (`--role`) in phase 1 or 2.
7. Payload sealing default for tenant feeds.
8. Partitions: per-feed key partitioning in v1 or later.
9. Whether the `feed` source is usable from `faucet run` without serve (recommended yes, with the shared lease).
10. Delete-by-key (data-subject deletion) on append-only backends: later phase; short retention is the v1 mitigation.

## Alternatives considered
| Alternative | Pros | Cons | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Forever-running webhook source** (never-ending run that flushes and keeps listening) | Small change to an existing connector | Fights the bounded-run model (state, exactly-once, governance per run); in-memory buffering; one process owns the endpoint (no HA) | Rejected |
| **Trigger body as data** (one run per webhook) | Very small change | One run and one sink commit per event: lake sinks get small-file/metadata explosion; heavy per-run overhead | Rejected (micro-batching required) |
| **"Use an external queue"** (Kafka/Redis/SQS in front, existing sources behind) | Works today, scales | Defeats "paste a URL" simplicity; extra infrastructure for low-volume senders | Kept as the documented high-volume path; feeds can later front an existing broker as a store backend |
| **Feeds writing directly to sinks** (no runs underneath) | Lower latency | A second delivery path that skips governance, DLQ, exactly-once, audit | Rejected (red line) |
| **One storage backend only** (e.g. Postgres) | Simpler | Locks out laptop use (SQLite), cheap long retention (object storage) and existing brokers | Rejected; pluggable `FeedStore` |
| **Continuous runs (epochs) instead of micro-runs** | Seconds-level latency | Larger engine change; not needed for minute-level use cases | Deferred; can replace micro-runs under the same feed layer |

## Risks
| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Skipped events from out-of-order commits (E1) | Safe-watermark invariant per backend + a conformance test that forces commit reordering |
| A stalled consumer silently loses data | Undelivered data is never deleted by age; hard cap refuses ingest (or drops with a visible gap marker); alerts at 50/80% |
| An internet-facing ingest surface | Write-only feed tokens, HMAC, Host/Origin allow-list, strict content types and limits, separate listener/host, data-at-rest protections (§11) |
| Scope creep into a broker or log shipper | Non-goals (§3); a high-volume path stays "use a broker" (optionally as a feed store backend) |
| Per-run overhead at small flush intervals | `min_interval`; continuous mode later for low latency |
| Storage growth / cost | Retention, quotas, `faucet_usage` metering of stored bytes |

## Assumptions
- Runs remain the only path that writes to sinks; `faucet_cli::runtime` stays the single entry point.
- The history DB (SQLite/Postgres) remains available as the place for feed metadata, leases and cursors.
- Event sizes are KB to low MB; larger payloads go to object storage (hybrid backend).
- Senders retry on non-2xx / timeouts at least a few times.

milestone.title: M10 - Import/Export & Backups
milestone.description:
Makes it practical to migrate from other budgeting tools and ensures data is never locked in. Users can bring their financial history in and take it out at any time.

- CSV and OFX/QFX transaction import with duplicate detection
- Full budget export including accounts, envelopes, and transaction history
- Import preview and conflict resolution UI
- Scheduled automated backup to local storage or object storage
- Import mapping profiles saved per institution

items.body:
## Summary

Each bank exports CSV differently. Without saved mapping profiles users must redo column mapping on every import. Nothing exists for this today; `accounts.institution` (`00016_add_account_institution.sql`) is the natural key to attach profiles to.

## Scope

**Backend**
- Migration: `import_mapping_profiles (id, budget_id NOT NULL, name TEXT NOT NULL, institution TEXT NULL, source_format TEXT CHECK IN ('csv','ofx','qfx'), mapping JSONB NOT NULL, detect_headers TEXT[] NULL, is_default BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false, created_by_user_id, created_at, updated_at, deleted_at)`. Unique `(budget_id, lower(name)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`. Profiles are budget-scoped, never user-scoped, per the tenant invariant.
- `mapping` schema: column indexes or header names for date/amount/debit/credit/payee/memo/external_id, date format, decimal and thousands separators, sign convention, header row offset, encoding. Validate with a Go struct and reject unknown keys.
- CRUD under `/api/v1/budgets/{budget_id}/import-profiles` (`authz.TransactionEdit` for writes, `TransactionView` for reads), soft delete, idempotent PUT/DELETE.
- Auto-detection: on upload, the importer compares the file's header row against each profile's `detect_headers` and the account's `institution`, and returns `suggested_profile_id` in the preview payload.
- Built-in starter profiles shipped as Go data (not DB rows) for a handful of common formats; copied into a budget on first use so users can edit them.
- Document in `docs/apis/09-import-export-api.md`.

**Web**
- `lib/api/import-profiles.ts`, `hooks/use-import-profiles.ts`.
- In the import stepper's mapping step: profile dropdown pre-selected from `suggested_profile_id`, "Save as profile" after mapping, and "Set as default for this institution".
- Management list in `DataPrivacyView.tsx` (or a new settings tab) to rename, edit, and delete profiles.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A saved profile applied to a second file from the same bank yields a correct preview with no manual mapping.
- [ ] Auto-detection suggests the right profile when headers match; no suggestion otherwise.
- [ ] Profiles are visible only inside their budget; the same user in another budget sees none.
- [ ] Invalid mapping JSON returns 400 with field errors.
- [ ] Re-deleting a deleted profile returns success.
- [ ] Repo, service, handler tests; web tests for the dropdown and save flow.

## Dependencies

- #448 (import pipeline), #450 (import preview UI)

## Suggested Labels

`enhancement`, `go`, `backend`, `web`

## Estimate

M

items.title: Simulated-live scheduled playback of a pre-recorded video as if it were live

labels.name: for consideration
labels.description: Idea parked for an owner decision before active work

items.body:
## ELI5
Pre-record your service, schedule it for 10am Sunday, and at 10am everyone's browser starts playing it together — synced. Someone joining at 10:15 drops into the video already 15 minutes in, just like real TV. Chat, prayer prompts, and Moments still fire at the right beats.

## Detailed proposal
New app/route `/simulated-live` (or extension to Livestream #273). Schema additions:

- `tblSimLiveEvents` — `eventId`, `siteId`, `recordingId` (FK → Recordings #264), `scheduledStart` (UTC), `durationSec`, `status` (`scheduled`/`live`/`ended`), `loop` (bool), `chatRoomId`, `createdBy`
- `tblSimLiveCues` — `eventId`, `offsetSec`, `cueType` (`moment`/`prayer-prompt`/`chat-pin`/`url`), `payload` (JSON) — fires server-side at offset

Server computes authoritative playhead: `playhead = now() - scheduledStart`. Client player (HLS or `<video>`) seeks to `playhead` on join, polls `/api/sim-live/{id}/state` every 10s for drift correction. Cues dispatched via existing notification/SSE channel.

Composes with: **Recordings #264** (source media), **Livestream #273** (chat room, viewer count, share UX), **Calendar** (schedule entry auto-creates sim-live event), **prayer-requests** (cue type triggers prompt overlay), **announcements** (post-event recap auto-published).

Admin UI: pick recording → pick datetime → optional cue timeline editor → publish. Public surface: same player chrome as livestream so attenders can't tell the difference.

## Pros
- Marquee COP-parity feature; differentiates from raw YouTube embed
- Solves replay-across-timezones (schedule same recording for AM Cambridge + PM US)
- Reuses Recordings + Livestream chat — no new chat infra
- Latecomer experience matches real broadcast (no "start from beginning" awkwardness)
- Cue system unlocks future interactivity (synced polls, giving prompts)

## Cons
- Server-authoritative time sync is fiddly across mobile-tab-backgrounding, network jitter, HLS segment boundaries
- HLS vs progressive MP4 decision affects seek accuracy and CDN cost
- Cue-firing reliability requires either SSE/WebSocket or aggressive polling — neither is free on shared hosting
- DRM/expiry: scheduled "premieres" of unreleased content need access control we don't have yet
- Admin UX for cue timeline is its own non-trivial editor

## How necessary?
Medium — high-value for multi-site / multi-timezone congregations and replay services; lower priority for single-service sites.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Admin can schedule a recording for a future datetime with optional loop flag
- [ ] At `scheduledStart`, all connected viewers begin playback synced within ±2s
- [ ] Latecomers seek to correct in-progress offset on join
- [ ] Chat room (from Livestream #273) is active for the duration of the event
- [ ] At least one cue type (Moment trigger) fires server-side at configured offset
- [ ] Event auto-transitions to `ended` and exposes recording for on-demand replay

## Estimated effort
4-5 days (sync engine + admin UI + cue dispatcher + player chrome reuse).

---

items.title: Multi-tenancy
[second-wave] Company configuration and custom fields
items.body:
Part of the second development wave — see #12 for why this is intentionally not on the critical path to pilots.

## What it is
Every trade business runs a little differently — this is about letting an org configure the platform to match their workflow instead of everyone getting the same fixed field set. This is also a prerequisite for a credible enterprise pitch: prospects will ask what's configurable before they'll commit to a migration.

## Scope (first pass)
- An org-level settings area (`/settings` or similar, admin+ only) covering things like: custom project statuses (beyond the current fixed `ProjectStatus` enum, or at least custom labels for them), custom fields on Project/Customer/Lead (a small, well-scoped set — not a full custom-schema builder), and branding basics (org logo/name as shown in the UI, eventually customer-facing surfaces).
- Custom fields should be additive metadata (e.g., a `Json` column or a `CustomFieldValue` table keyed by field definition), not schema migrations per org — this needs to stay multi-tenant-safe without an org's config affecting others.

## Explicitly out of scope for v1
- Fully custom workflows/pipelines (e.g., arbitrary lead status transitions) — start with configurable labels, not configurable state machines
- White-labeling beyond basic branding (custom domains, etc.)

## Depends on / relates to
- Integrations/API issue (#see) — API key management likely lives in this same settings area

labels.description: Parent work item with phase sub-issues

items.body:
# Security & Observability Enhancements

## Context / Spec

# Security & Observability Enhancements

## Objective
Provide comprehensive security hardening and observability infrastructure across the MoonWitness & Empire of the Light ecosystem, ensuring all applications enforce tenant isolation, auditability, and production-grade observability while maintaining compatibility with the seven-world DNA skin system.

## Problem Statement
The monorepo currently lacks unified security and observability primitives. Individual apps implement basic logging and error handling, but there is no shared framework for:
- Centralized audit logging with tamper-evident records
- Tenant isolation enforcement across all data operations
- Security metrics and alerting infrastructure
- Production readiness validation gates
- Integration with the existing DNA skin engine for consistent security UX

## Objectives & Expected Outcomes
- Deploy a shared audit logging service with append-only event storage
- Enforce tenant_id derivation from authenticated principal (never from request body)
- Provide standardized security middleware for all hub routes
- Implement observability dashboards for request tracing, error rates, and security events
- Ensure all model operations (insert/update/delete) write audit events in the same transaction
- Create production readiness gates that verify security and observability compliance

## Functional Requirements
1. **Audit Logging Service**: Shared service that records every model insert/update/delete with changed field names (not values), tenant_id, actor identity, and timestamp in append-only storage
2. **Tenant Isolation Middleware**: Automatic derivation and validation of company_id on every row; fail-closed rejection on legal_hold / retention_until
3. **Security Middleware**: Default-deny auth policy for hub routes; explicit public allowlist (`/health`, `/ready`, onboarding, non-prod `/docs`)
4. **Observability Pipeline**: Structured logging (JSON format), request ID propagation, error boundary reporting, and Prometheus-compatible metrics
5. **Production Readiness Gates**: Automated checks that verify audit logging, tenant isolation, and security middleware are properly configured before deployment

## Non-Functional Requirements
- All audit events must be SHA-256 content-addressed and stored in `data/storage/<digest>`
- Zero secret leakage in logs (redact all `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` values carrying keys/secrets/tokens)
- Performance impact < 5ms per request for security middleware
- Observability data must not block primary request flow
- Compatibility with all seven DNA skin worlds (Imperium Lumen, Nexus Paradox, Lunar Chronicles, etc.)

## Scope
- Shared libraries: `@moonwitness/lint` architecture checks, audit logging service, tenant isolation middleware
- Affected apps: dock, headquarter, id, jizz, moonsky, harbor, gate, sentinel, server
- Integration with `@allah/arsy-orm` for embedded PGlite audit event storage
- Compliance with MOONFRAME SKIN ENGINE contract (token domains, motion, responsive behavior)

## Out-of-Scope
- Application-level business logic changes
- Database schema migrations beyond audit event table
- Third-party security tool integration (self-hosted only)
- Client-side secret management (remains server-authoritative)

## User Stories & Use Cases
1. **Developer**: "When I create a new service, the system automatically logs the creation event with tenant context, and I can query audit events without exposing raw data."
2. **Operator**: "When a suspicious operation occurs, the observability dashboard shows the request ID, affected tenant, and security context for investigation."
3. **Operator**: "When a tenant is on legal_hold, all write operations are rejected with a fail-closed error, and the audit log records the rejection."
4. **Designer**: "Security error pages and audit views use the approved DNA skin tokens and composition blocks, ensuring visual consistency across all seven worlds."

## Dependencies & Constraints
- `@allah/arsy-orm` embedded PGlite for audit event storage
- `@moonwitness/ui` composition blocks (header, destination-card, section-heading, route-shell, status-message, state-panel, kicker)
- MOONFRAME SKIN ENGINE contract token domains and invariants
- Existing `data/storage/` content-addressed storage pattern
- `lint:arch` architecture invariant checks
- `pnpm verify:release` full release gate

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Audit logging service is operational and records all model lifecycle events with tenant_id and actor identity
- [ ] Tenant isolation middleware enforces company_id on every row and rejects operations on legal_hold/retention_until tenants
- [ ] Security middleware implements default-deny auth policy with explicit public allowlist
- [ ] Observability pipeline provides structured JSON logging, request ID propagation, and Prometheus metrics
- [ ] Production readiness gates pass: `pnpm verify:fast` and `pnpm verify:release` succeed
- [ ] All seven DNA skin worlds render security and observability UX consistently
- [ ] No `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` values carrying secrets reach the browser
- [ ] `pnpm lint:arch` passes with zero warnings for security/observability changes

## Success Metrics
- 100% of model insert/update/delete operations write audit events in the same transaction
- Zero audit events contain unredacted secret material
- < 5ms overhead for security middleware per request
- All quality gates (`pnpm docs:check`, `pnpm contract:check`, `pnpm lint:arch`, `pnpm typecheck`) pass
- Production deployment can be blocked by readiness gate failures

## Design

# Design: Security & Observability Enhancements

## High-Level Architecture

The architecture introduces three new shared layers integrated with the existing MoonWitness ecosystem:

### 1. Audit Log Service Layer
- **Location**: `packages/lint/src/audit-service.ts` (new) + `packages/arsy-orm` integration
- **Pattern**: Append-only event storage with SHA-256 content addressing
- **Storage**: `data/storage/<digest>` per the content-addressed storage contract
- **Event Schema**: `{ id, timestamp, tenant_id, actor, action, resource_type, resource_id, changed_fields, old_values_hash, new_values_hash, ip_address, user_agent }`
- **Transaction**: Every model insert/update/delete writes one append-only event in the same transaction

### 2. Tenant Isolation Middleware Layer
- **Location**: `packages/lint/src/tenant-middleware.ts` (new)
- **Pattern**: Middleware that runs before every route handler
- **Resolution**: `company_id` derived from authenticated principal, never from request body
- **Fail-Closed**: Reject operations on `legal_hold` / `retention_until` tenants
- **Allowlist**: Explicit public routes (`/health`, `/ready`, onboarding, non-prod `/docs`)

### 3. Observability Pipeline Layer
- **Location**: `packages/lint/src/observability.ts` (new)
- **Pattern**: Structured logging, request ID propagation, metrics emission
- **Logging**: JSON format with correlated fields (request_id, tenant_id, span_id, trace_id)
- **Metrics**: Prometheus-compatible counters for requests, errors, security events
- **Tracing**: OpenTelemetry-compatible request spans with baggage propagation

### Integration Points
- **DNA Skin Engine**: Security and observability UX uses `@moonwitness/ui` composition blocks
  - `route-shell.tsx` for security error pages
  - `state-panel.tsx` for audit event browsing
  - `destination-card.tsx` for summary views
  - `section-heading.tsx` for section headers
- **ARSY-ORM**: Audit events stored alongside ORM operations via PGlite
- **All apps**: Security middleware applied at the hub route level; observability configured per app

## Component & Module Structure

### New Packages/Modules
- `packages/lint/src/audit-service.ts` - Audit logging service
- `packages/lint/src/tenant-middleware.ts` - Tenant isolation middleware
- `packages/lint/src/observability.ts` - Observability pipeline

### Modified Packages
- `packages/arsy-orm` - Extended to automatically write audit events on model lifecycle
- `packages/ui/src/blocks/` - Existing composition blocks used for security UX
- `packages/types` - Updated type definitions for audit events and tenant contexts

### Package Boundaries & Responsibilities
- **`@moonwitness/lint`**: Architecture invariants, audit service, tenant middleware, observability pipeline
- **`@allah/arsy-orm`**: ORM operations + automatic audit event injection
- **`@moonwitness/ui`**: UI composition blocks for security/observability views
- **App packages**: Apply middleware and configure observability; no internal logic changes

## Data Models & Relationships

### Audit Event Model
```typescript
interface AuditEvent {
  id: string;                          // SHA-256 digest
  timestamp: string;                   // ISO 8601
  tenant_id: string;                   // Derived from principal
  actor: string;                       // User/service identity
  action: 'CREATE' | 'UPDATE' | 'DELETE';
  resource_type: string;               // e.g., 'service', 'environment', 'key'
  resource_id: string;                 // ORM record ID
  changed_fields: string[];            // Field names that changed (not values)
  old_values_hash: string;             // SHA-256 of previous state (empty for CREATE)
  new_values_hash: string;             // SHA-256 of current state
  ip_address: string;                  // Client or request source
  user_agent: string;                  // Browser/service identifier
}
```

### Tenant Context Model
```typescript
interface TenantContext {
  company_id: string;                  // Derived from authenticated principal
  legal_hold: boolean;                  // Fail-closed rejection flag
  retention_until: string | null;      // Fail-closed rejection flag
  approved_roles: string[];            // Allowed operations for this tenant
}
```

## API Contracts & Interfaces

### Audit Service API
```typescript
// Log a model lifecycle event
auditService.log({
  action: 'CREATE' | 'UPDATE' | 'DELETE',
  resourceType: string,
  resourceId: string,
  changedFields: string[],
  oldValues?: Record<string, unknown>,
  newValues?: Record<string, unknown>,
  actor: string;
})

// Get audit events with filtering
auditService.getEvents({
  tenantId?: string,
  action?: string,
  resourceType?: string,
  startDate?: string,
  endDate?: string,
  limit?: number,
  offset?: number;
})
```

### Tenant Middleware API
```typescript
// Use in route handlers
const tenant = requireTenant();  // Returns TenantContext, throws if fail-closed
const isPublic = isPublicRoute();  // Checks allowlist
```

### Observability API
```typescript
// Start a traced request
observability.startRequest({ path, method, tenantId });

// Log an event within the request
observability.log({ level, message, correlationId });

// Emit a metric
observability.metric({ name, value, labels });

// End the request span
observability.endRequest({ success, error });
```

## Data Flow & System Interactions

### Model Lifecycle → Audit Event Flow
1. User/Service initiates model operation (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE)
2. `arsy-orm` transaction begins
3. Operation executes on PGlite
4. If successful, `auditService.log()` is called with:
   - Action type
   - Resource type/id
   - Changed field names (not values)
   - Old and new value hashes
   - Tenant context (from principal)
   - Actor identity
5. Audit event stored in `data/storage/<digest>` (append-only)
6. Transaction commits (including audit event)
7. Observability pipeline records the event via `observability.log()`

### Request Flow → Security + Observability
1. Incoming request hits hub route
2. `tenant-middleware` runs first:
   - Derives `company_id` from authenticated principal
   - Checks `legal_hold` / `retention_until` - rejects if set
   - Validates route is in public allowlist if anonymous
3. `observability.startRequest()` begins span
4. Route handler executes
5. `observability.endRequest()` finishes span with success/error status
6. Response sent with security headers and observability data attached

### Error Flow
1. Any error during above flows triggers `observability.log({ level: 'error', ... })`
2. Error boundary renders DNA-appropriate error page (using `@moonwitness/ui` StatePanel)
3. Audit event with `action: 'ERROR'` is logged if operation partially completed
4. Fail-closed tenant checks ensure no data leakage on errors

## UI/UX Flows & Design Specifications

### Security Error Pages
- Built from `StatePanel` (`STATE_PARITY` invariant)
- Uses DNA-appropriate skin tokens from `packages/ui/src/theme.css`
- Consistent across all seven worlds (Imperium Lumen, Nexus Paradox, etc.)
- Shows generic error message; detailed logging internal only

### Audit View Component Tree
```
RouteShell
  └─ Kicker (optional)
  └─ SectionHeading ("Audit Log")
  └─ DestinationCard (summary statistics)
  └─ StatePanel (audit event browser with filtering)
      ├─ EmptyState (no events yet)
      ├─ LoadingState (fetching events)
      └─ ErrorState (fetch failed)
          └─ FilterControls (tenant, action, date range)
```

### Observability Dashboard
- Minimalist design using `@moonwitness/ui` tokens
- Time-series graphs for request rate, error rate, security events
- Drill-down by tenant, IP, or action type
- Responsive: wide (desktop), medium (tablet), narrow (mobile), touch modes

## Integration Architecture

### Skin Integration
Each app declares a `SkinRoot`; security and observability views use:
- `SkinScope` for route-specific experiences without duplicate root worlds
- Token-driven utilities from `packages/ui/src/theme.css`
- Consistent component composition via `@moonwitness/ui`

### Cross-Application Consistency
- Security middleware: Same implementation in all apps
- Observability pipeline: Same configuration pattern across apps
- Audit service: Centralized shared service, not duplicated per app
- Tenant isolation: Derived from principal; same logic in all apps

### Error Handling & Failure Scenarios

#### Audit Service Failures
- **Database unavailable**: Cache miss; retry with exponential backoff; event lost but not leaked
- **Append-only violation**: Alert operator; halt non-critical operations until resolved
- **Performance degradation**: Batch events; reduce flush frequency; alert on latency threshold

#### Tenant Middleware Failures
- **Principal resolution failure**: Default-deny; route to `/ready` with authentication required
- **legal_hold edge case**: Log the edge case; require explicit admin override (recorded in audit)
- **Tenant context stale**: Refresh from principal; if still invalid, fail-closed

#### Observability Pipeline Failures
- **Logger unavailable**: Buffer events in memory; flush on recovery; do not block request
- **Metric emission failure**: Best-effort only; do not throw; internal alerting
- **Tracing propagation failure**: Continue without trace context; mark spans as incomplete

## Security & Performance Considerations

### Security
- **Secret redaction**: All `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` values carrying keys/secrets/tokens are stripped from logs
- **Tenant fail-closed**: `legal_hold` / `retention_until` always reject; never implicit allow
- **Default-deny auth**: Every hub route needs verified principal; explicit allowlist only
- **Content-addressed storage**: SHA-256 digests prevent tampering; events are immutable
- **No cross-skin state leakage**: Each skin's security UX is independent; no shared state

### Performance
- **Security middleware**: < 5ms overhead per request (middleware only, no DB calls)
- **Audit event writing**: Within same transaction as ORM operation; no additional round-trips
- **Observability logging**: JSON format; batched flush every 1s or 100 events; async
- **Metric emission**: Non-blocking; in-process counters with periodic export
- **Content-addressed storage**: SHA-256 computation only; no external service dependencies

## Observability Strategy

### Logging
- Structured JSON logs with correlation IDs
- Fields: `timestamp, level, message, request_id, tenant_id, span_id, trace_id, action, result`
- Output: Centralized log aggregator (ELK, Loki, or similar)
- Redaction: Automated stripping of secret-carrying environment variables

### Metrics (Prometheus-Compatible)
- `moonwitness_requests_total`: Total requests by method, path, status code
- `moonwitness_request_duration_seconds`: Request latency histogram
- `moonwitness_audit_events_total`: Audit events by action, resource_type, result
- `moonwitness_tenant_violations_total`: Tenant isolation violations (legal_hold, etc.)
- `moonwitness_security_errors_total`: Security middleware errors

### Tracing
- OpenTelemetry-compatible request spans
- Baggage: `tenant_id`, `actor_id`, `correlation_id`
- Propagation: W3C Trace Context (traceparent header)
- Sampling: Probabilistic 10% for high-volume routes, 100% for security-sensitive routes

## Technical Decisions & Alternatives Considered

### Decision: Shared audit service vs. per-app logging
**Chosen**: Shared service in `@moonwitness/lint` with arsy-orm integration
**Rejected**: Per-app logging (violates audit invariants, duplication risk)
**Rationale**: Single source of truth ensures consistency; arsy-orm integration makes audit automatic

### Decision: Tenant ID from principal vs. from request
**Chosen**: Derived from authenticated principal (fail-closed)
**Rejected**: From request body/query parameters (insecure, violates invariants)
**Rationale**: Invariants explicitly state `company_id` derived from principal, fail-closed

### Decision: Append-only event storage vs. mutable audit log
**Chosen**: Append-only in `data/storage/<digest>`
**Rejected**: Database table with UPDATE/DELETE operations
**Rationale**: Tamper-evident; aligns with content-addressed storage contract; simplifies recovery

### Decision: JSON logging vs. text-based logging
**Chosen**: JSON format with structured fields
**Rejected**: Free-form text logs
**Rationale**: Machine-parseable; enables metrics and tracing; standardized across ecosystem

### Decision: SHA-256 digest vs. UUID for audit event IDs
**Chosen**: SHA-256 content-addressed digest
**Rejected**: UUID v4
**Rationale**: Tamper-evident; content-addressed storage pattern; verifiable integrity

## Rules / Invariants

# Security & Observability Rules

## Security boundaries

- Every hub route is default-deny and requires a verified principal unless it is on the explicit public allowlist: `/health`, `/ready`, onboarding, and non-production `/docs`.
- Derive `company_id` from the authenticated principal for every tenant-scoped row. Never accept tenant identity from request data.
- Reject writes when `legal_hold` is active or `retention_until` has not elapsed. Fail closed when tenant or retention state cannot be verified.
- Authorize global-admin access on each admin route, require a reason, and record the target tenant. Generic CRUD must not expose identity, audit, or credential-bearing models.
- Use `@allah/arsy-orm` with embedded PGlite for persistence. Parameterize SQL values and allowlist dynamic identifiers.

## Audit and storage

- Record one append-only audit event for each model insert, update, and delete in the same transaction as the model change.
- Include changed field names, actor, and principal-derived `company_id`; do not store changed values or secrets in audit events.
- Store audit content using SHA-256 content addressing at `data/storage/<digest>`. Keep stored content write-once.
- Audit failures must fail the model transaction rather than report a successful unaudited write.

## Observability and secrets

- Emit structured logs and propagate request identifiers without placing credentials, tokens, secret values, or raw changed values in logs, metrics, or traces.
- Keep observability best-effort so an exporter failure does not block the primary request, while preserving security and audit transaction failures.
- Restrict metric labels and trace attributes to bounded, non-secret fields. Do not use tenant identifiers or other high-cardinality values as metric labels.
- Keep upstream credentials server-side. Client code must not read `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` values that carry keys, secrets, or tokens.

## Delivery constraints

- Use the existing architecture and platform contracts as the source of truth; do not introduce a second ORM, storage model, UI control system, or client-to-hub transport.
- Apply security and observability at shared boundaries where possible. Do not change unrelated application business behavior.
- Measure performance claims and security coverage; do not treat the plan's targets as verified results until tests or runtime evidence support them.
- UI changes must use `@moonwitness/ui`, skin tokens, and the existing route-state patterns. Do not add raw controls, private component-class selectors, or palette colors in app markup.
- Verify relevant contracts, architecture checks, tests, and type checks for each implementation slice. Report checks that were not run.


## Phases

# Tasks: Security & Observability Enhancements

- [ ] #425 Phase 1 — Audit Logging Service Foundation
- [ ] #426 Phase 2 — Tenant Isolation Middleware
- [ ] #427 Phase 3 — Observability Pipeline
- [ ] #428 Phase 4 — Production Readiness Gates & Integration
- [ ] #429 Phase 5 — Documentation & Type Safety
- [ ] #430 Completion Checklist
