type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Situation

AdminConnect manages tenants, plans and entitlements, but nothing reports on the commercial state of the subscription base. The platform sells on several dimensions at once — clinic, hospital, enterprise and government plans, priced per bed, per facility, per user, per module and on usage — and today the only way to answer "what is our MRR, which tenants are in trial, and which renewals are at risk this quarter" is to query the billing control plane by hand and reconcile it against the entitlement tables in a spreadsheet.

The consequence of the absence is commercial rather than clinical, but it is not minor. Nobody sees a trial expiring without conversion until it has expired. Nobody sees that a hospital tenant grew from 120 to 190 licensed beds and is being billed for 120, which is straightforward revenue leakage on a per-bed plan. Nobody sees a failed UPI AutoPay mandate until the account is already in arrears, and because UPI AutoPay mandates carry a fixed maximum amount, an upgrade that pushes a tenant's charge above the mandate cap will silently fail collection every cycle until someone notices. Affected roles are the platform commercial team, the customer-success owner for each tenant, and the finance lead who reports MRR and churn to the board.

There is a hard architectural constraint. Subscription data lives in the shared control plane, which under the data-residency rule (BRIEF §3) may hold billing metadata and feature configuration only. This dashboard must therefore be built entirely from tenant-level commercial facts — plan, entitlement counts, invoice totals, mandate state, aggregate usage counters — and must never reach into a country data store for anything patient-related. GST treatment also differs for SaaS supply versus medicine supply, so subscription revenue must be reported separately from any hospital-side revenue figure.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** platform commercial lead
**I want** a subscription dashboard covering recurring revenue, plan and pricing-dimension mix, trial conversion, renewal risk, entitlement overage and mandate health
**So that** trials, renewals, overages and failed mandates are acted on inside the cycle they occur rather than discovered after revenue is lost.

### Scope

**In scope**

* Subscription fact tables in the control-plane analytics store, fed from subscription and payment domain events by an idempotent Go consumer.
* Recurring revenue metrics: MRR, ARR, new / expansion / contraction / churned MRR movement, net revenue retention, and average revenue per tenant.
* Plan and pricing-dimension mix: tenants and MRR split by plan tier and by billing dimension (per-bed, per-facility, per-user, per-module, usage-based).
* Trial funnel: active trials, days remaining, conversion rate and time-to-convert, with a list of trials expiring inside the next 14 days.
* Renewal pipeline: contracts by renewal date, renewal risk indicator derived from usage decline, support-ticket volume and payment failures.
* Entitlement overage detection: licensed versus actually consumed beds, facilities, users and enabled modules, with the billable delta.
* Mandate and dunning health: UPI AutoPay mandate state, mandate cap headroom against the next charge, failed collections and dunning stage.
* OpenFGA authorisation restricting the dashboard to platform commercial, finance and executive roles, with no tenant-user access at all.

**Out of scope**

* Subscription invoice generation, proration, credit notes and dunning execution — these belong to the Commercial Platform team's Subscriptions epic; this issue reports on their output.
* Platform infrastructure health, latency SLOs and quota consumption — owned by #582.
* Hospital-side revenue, payer mix and receivables — owned by #385 and #580; hospital revenue and platform subscription revenue are never combined in a single figure.
* Compliance and regulatory reporting for tenants — owned by #591.
* Scheduled delivery of subscription summaries to the commercial team — owned by #593.

---

## Recommended Solution

A `subscription-analytics` Go module inside the control plane, consuming a durable NATS JetStream pull consumer on `platform.subscription.*` and `platform.billing.*` and writing to a dedicated analytics schema in the control-plane PostgreSQL 16 cluster. Because the control plane is the only store that legitimately holds cross-country tenant data, this is the one analytics surface that is deliberately global — and it is therefore the one that must be checked hardest for accidental PHI ingress. A schema-level constraint enforces that: every column in `analytics.fact_subscription_*` is either an identifier, a code, a count or an integer minor-unit amount. No free text, no patient or practitioner identifiers, no facility address.

**Data model:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE analytics.dim_tenant (
  tenant_key      serial PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  country_profile text NOT NULL,            -- IN now; NP/AF later
  segment         text NOT NULL CHECK (segment IN
                    ('clinic','hospital','enterprise','government')),
  onboarded_on    date NOT NULL,
  valid_from      timestamptz NOT NULL,
  valid_to        timestamptz,              -- SCD type 2
  is_current      boolean NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE analytics.fact_subscription_state (
  snapshot_date_key int  NOT NULL REFERENCES analytics.dim_date,
  tenant_key      int    NOT NULL REFERENCES analytics.dim_tenant,
  plan_code       text   NOT NULL,
  lifecycle       text   NOT NULL CHECK (lifecycle IN
                    ('trial','active','past_due','suspended','churned')),
  trial_ends_on   date,
  renews_on       date,
  mrr_paise       bigint NOT NULL,
  licensed_beds   int, licensed_facilities int, licensed_users int,
  consumed_beds   int, consumed_facilities int, consumed_users int,
  enabled_modules text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  mandate_state   text CHECK (mandate_state IN
                    ('none','active','paused','revoked','expired','failed')),
  mandate_cap_paise bigint,
  PRIMARY KEY (snapshot_date_key, tenant_key)
);

CREATE TABLE analytics.fact_mrr_movement (
  movement_key bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_key   int    NOT NULL REFERENCES analytics.dim_tenant,
  period_key   int    NOT NULL,
  movement     text   NOT NULL CHECK (movement IN
                 ('new','expansion','contraction','churn','reactivation')),
  delta_paise  bigint NOT NULL,
  reason_code  text,
  source_event_id uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
```

`fact_subscription_state` is a **daily snapshot** rather than a computed-on-read view. MRR as at a past date cannot be reconstructed once plans change, and board reporting must reproduce last quarter's number exactly. A Temporal scheduled workflow writes one row per tenant per day and derives the movement rows by differencing consecutive snapshots, so MRR movement always sums back to the change in total MRR — a property asserted in test rather than assumed.

Overage is computed in the snapshot, not in the UI: `consumed_* - licensed_*` per dimension, with counts sourced from `EntitlementUsageReported` events that each country deployment publishes upward as bare integers. That upward flow is the only data path from a country store to the control plane, and it carries counts only.

**API surface:**

* `GET /api/v1/admin/subscriptions/summary?as_of=` — MRR, ARR, tenant counts by lifecycle.
* `GET /api/v1/admin/subscriptions/mrr-movement?from=&to=` — new/expansion/contraction/churn waterfall.
* `GET /api/v1/admin/subscriptions/mix?dimension=plan|segment|billing_dimension|country`
* `GET /api/v1/admin/subscriptions/trials?expiring_within_days=`
* `GET /api/v1/admin/subscriptions/renewals?from=&to=&risk=at_risk|all`
* `GET /api/v1/admin/subscriptions/overage?min_delta=`
* `GET /api/v1/admin/subscriptions/mandates?state=failed|cap_breach_risk`
* `GET /api/v1/admin/subscriptions/tenants/{tenant_id}/timeline` — plan, movement and payment history for one tenant.

**Events consumed:** `SubscriptionCreated`, `TrialStarted`, `TrialConverted`, `TrialExpired`, `PlanChanged`, `SubscriptionSuspended`, `SubscriptionCancelled`, `EntitlementUsageReported`, `SubscriptionInvoiceIssued`, `SubscriptionPaymentSucceeded`, `SubscriptionPaymentFailed`, `MandateStateChanged`. **Published:** `SubscriptionOverageDetected`, `MandateCapBreachRisk`, `TrialExpiringSoon` — these are emitted by the analytics module because it is the only component that sees the derived condition, and customer success consumes them for outreach.

**OpenFGA:**

```
type subscription_report
  relations
    define platform: [platform]
    define viewer:   commercial_lead from platform
                  or platform_finance from platform
                  or executive from platform
    define tenant_detail_viewer: commercial_lead from platform
                  or csm_assigned from platform
    define exporter: platform_finance from platform
```

There is deliberately no relation granting a tenant user access. A hospital administrator must not be able to see the plan mix or MRR of other tenants, and the cleanest way to guarantee that is to give tenant roles no path to this type at all rather than to filter results.

**Sequencing.** Depends on the Subscriptions epic emitting the lifecycle and mandate events above with stable reason codes, and on each country deployment publishing `EntitlementUsageReported`. Reuse `analytics.dim_date` from #385 rather than defining a second date dimension. #582 is independent and can land in parallel; the two dashboards share the AdminConnect platform-console shell but no data.

**Risks.** Mid-cycle plan changes make MRR ambiguous — resolved by defining MRR as normalised monthly value of the plan in force at snapshot time, documented on the dashboard, with the waterfall reconciling to it. Multi-currency is a latent trap once Nepal and Afghanistan profiles land — amounts are stored in minor units with an explicit `currency` on the plan and MRR is only ever aggregated after conversion at a dated rate, never by summing raw minor units. Usage-based lines arriving late would restate a closed period, so usage is billed and reported one period in arrears with the period stamped as provisional until its usage window closes.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a control plane with 40 tenants across clinic, hospital and enterprise plans, including six active trials and three tenants consuming more beds than licensed
**When** the commercial lead opens the subscription dashboard for the current month
**Then** total MRR is shown with a new/expansion/contraction/churn waterfall that sums exactly to the difference from the prior month's closing MRR, the six trials are listed with days remaining and conversion status, and the three overage tenants are listed with the per-dimension billable delta.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** a tenant on per-bed pricing whose next scheduled charge of ₹84,000 exceeds their active UPI AutoPay mandate cap of ₹75,000
**When** the mandate health panel is rendered and the nightly snapshot runs
**Then** the tenant appears under cap-breach risk with both amounts shown, `MandateCapBreachRisk` is published for customer-success outreach, and the account is flagged before the collection attempt rather than after it fails.

### Edge Cases

* A tenant churns and reactivates in the same month — the waterfall records a churn and a reactivation movement, and net MRR movement matches the snapshot difference rather than double-counting.
* A `SubscriptionPaymentFailed` event is redelivered by JetStream — the `source_event_id` unique constraint makes it a no-op and the dunning stage does not advance twice.
* An enterprise tenant on schema-per-tenant isolation reports entitlement usage from two country deployments — counts aggregate per tenant but the country split remains visible, and no country's figures are merged into another's data store.
* A trial expires with no conversion decision recorded — it is counted as an expired trial, not as churn, so churned MRR is not inflated by revenue that never existed.
* A government tenant is billed annually in advance — MRR is the normalised monthly value, and the annual invoice does not appear as a one-month revenue spike.
* A platform engineer with `#582` operations access but no commercial relation requests the MRR summary — the request is denied at the OpenFGA check, not filtered in the handler.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team's agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team's agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** the commercial team works trials, renewals, overages and failed mandates from a single dashboard, with each list actionable down to the named tenant.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** entitlement overage and mandate failures are detected in the cycle they arise, closing the two largest sources of silent revenue leakage on multi-dimension pricing.
* **Success metric or validation method:** MRR waterfall reconciles to snapshot-difference MRR to the paise across a 90-day backfill; every trial expiring within 14 days appears on the dashboard at least 14 days ahead with zero misses over a quarter; overage detection identifies 100% of seeded entitlement breaches in test; dashboard p95 under 1.5s at 500 tenants; adversarial tests confirm no tenant-scoped principal can reach any endpoint in this module.
* **Monitoring period, where applicable:** one full quarterly close, tracking snapshot job success rate, waterfall reconciliation variance (target zero), and the count of overages converted to billed revenue.

---


---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions


## Exceptions

None — all guardrails apply. Tenant isolation is tested as an all-or-nothing boundary here rather than a row filter, since no tenant principal should reach this surface at all, and the control plane's prohibition on holding PHI is asserted by an automated schema check in CI as part of the security guardrail.

items.title: R-Co's adp-0x tenant-modeling design docs are stale relative to R-Co's actual schema-per-tenant implementation
items.body:
R-Co's six src/design/adp-0x*.md documents (adp-01-tenant-column-event-store.md, adp-02-tenant-columns-definition-instance-audit.md, adp-03-tenant-context-resolution-api.md, adp-04-user-tenant-binding.md, adp-04a-external-identity-linkage-user.md, adp-04b-tenant-realm-binding.md) all describe the same additive tenant_id-column-in-one-shared-schema multi-tenancy model. None of the six, read in full this session, mentions schema-per-tenant, a tenant_schemas registry table, or a per-tenant schema-provisioning function anywhere in their text.

R-Co's actual migration history (verified directly this session against C:\Users\tvolo\dev\ai-dala\R-Co\migrations\) shows R-Co later layered a second, orthogonal isolation mechanism on top of the tenant-column pattern:

- migrations/060_schema_per_tenant_bootstrap.sql (tagged SPT-01) creates a public.tenant_schemas registry and a public.bpm_provision_tenant_schema(p_tenant_id UUID) function that provisions a real Postgres schema per tenant, and widens public.schema_migrations's primary key to (schema_name, version)
- migrations/GBL-112_tnt01_drop_legacy_public_business_tables.sql drops 19 named legacy public-schema business tables that migrations 001-059 had created before migration 060 existed
- src/db/migrations.zig's runForSchema replays the migration set once per registered tenant schema under a search_path of <schema>,public
- iss0150-gh482-20260810-adp0x-schema-fix.md documents six broken R-Co integration tests that assumed table_schema = 'public' for tables that actually live under tenant_default/per-tenant schemas post-GBL-112 — direct catalog-level confirmation the cutover is real and complete, not aspirational
- 1147_par01_events_partitioning.sql explicitly classifies events/events_archive as PER_TENANT in R-Co's own dual-schema classification scheme

The adp-0x docs were seemingly never updated to reflect this shift — they describe R-Co's tenant-modeling approach as it stood at an earlier point in its evolution, not its current, actual state. A future reader of the adp-0x docs alone (without also reading the migration history) would be misled into thinking R-Co's isolation model is tenant-column-only, when the current reality is schema-per-tenant with tenant_id columns retained as an intra-schema mechanism.

This is a documentation-currency problem in R-Co's own src/design/ tree, not a Letflow-side defect, and is out of scope for Letflow's own pipeline to fix in R-Co's repository. Recorded here so a future reader isn't misled the same way this design's first read (lib/letflow/design/0003-ecto-schema-strategy-decision.md section 2.2) nearly was. Letflow's own docs/migration/decisions/0003-ecto-schema-strategy.md now explicitly reasons from R-Co's actual current implementation rather than the adp-0x docs alone.

Discovered by ELIXIR-DEV during WF02-REQ012.
Local record: docs/issues/ISS-0005.yaml

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Situation

The platform runs a single PostgreSQL 16 primary per country under CloudNativePG, serving every read and write for every tenant across all eleven products. There are no read replicas in the query path, no partitioning on the tables that grow without bound, no connection pooler between hundreds of Go service replicas and a fixed backend limit, and no plan for what happens when a single hospital group's data outgrows what one instance can serve.

This is a hard ceiling, not a gradual degradation. PostgreSQL allocates a backend process per connection; a Kubernetes deployment that scales to 60 pods with a 20-connection GORM pool each demands 1,200 backends against a `max_connections` that cannot safely be set anywhere near that. The failure mode is not slowness — it is `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`, returned to a **ward nurse** mid-drug-round and an **ambulance dispatcher** mid-dispatch, at exactly the moment autoscaling responds to load. KEDA scaling the API tier under load will, without a pooler, actively cause the outage it is trying to prevent.

The growth profile makes partitioning unavoidable. Observations, audit records, appointment history and billing transaction lines grow monotonically and are never deleted — audit records specifically cannot be deleted, because tamper-evident audit of record access, prescriptions, billing and break-glass access is an architectural requirement, and CERT-In imposes log-retention obligations independently. A single unpartitioned `observation` table across a multi-hospital tenant reaches hundreds of millions of rows within two years, at which point autovacuum, index maintenance and any query that is not a perfect index hit all degrade together.

There is a correctness dimension too. Row-level security is the platform's primary tenant boundary, and RLS predicates interact badly with poorly planned queries: a policy that the planner cannot push down turns a targeted index scan into a full scan with a filter, which is both slow and a warning sign. Adding replicas introduces replication lag, and a read-after-write race on a clinical record — a doctor saving a note and immediately not seeing it — is a safety and trust problem, not a caching nicety.

Affected roles: every clinical and operational user of the platform, the SRE on call, the DPO whose audit and retention obligations depend on these tables remaining queryable, and hospital administrators of large groups whose data volume is the growth case.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** platform SRE
**I want** connection pooling, read replicas with explicit consistency routing, partitioning of unbounded tables, and a defined path to physical isolation for large tenants
**So that** the database scales with tenant growth and API autoscaling without connection exhaustion, unbounded table growth or a read-after-write hazard on clinical data.

### Scope

**In scope**

* PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode between application replicas and the CloudNativePG cluster, with pool sizing derived from backend capacity rather than replica count, and prepared-statement handling made compatible with GORM.
* Streaming read replicas, with an explicit routing policy in the tenant-scoped data access layer: reads are replica-eligible only when a handler declares tolerance for staleness, and everything else goes to the primary.
* A read-your-writes mechanism using the write LSN carried in the request context, so a session that has written is pinned to the primary or waits for the replica to catch up rather than silently serving stale clinical data.
* Declarative range partitioning by time on `observation`, `audit_record`, `encounter_event`, `billing_transaction_line` and `notification_log`, with automated partition creation and detachment, and constraint exclusion verified in query plans.
* Index review across the highest-traffic tables including partial and covering indexes, removal of unused and duplicate indexes, and a policy that all new indexes are created concurrently.
* RLS policy plan verification: an automated check asserting that tenant-scoped queries on the largest tables produce index scans with the tenant predicate pushed down, failing CI when a plan regresses to a sequential scan.
* Autovacuum and statistics tuning per table class, with aggressive settings on high-churn tables such as the appointment and work-order tables.
* Statement timeout, idle-in-transaction timeout and lock timeout set per connection role, so a runaway analytical query cannot hold locks against clinical writes.
* A documented and rehearsed migration path to schema-per-tenant and database-per-tenant for enterprise-tier hospitals, including the tenant-move procedure.

**Out of scope**

* Application-level latency budgets, rate limiting and the CI performance gate — owned by #595.
* Redis caching topology and cache invalidation — owned by #597; the read-replica policy here defines what may be cached at all.
* Search index performance — owned by #598.
* Cross-zone database failover and standby placement — owned by #601.
* Backup, restore, point-in-time recovery and RPO/RTO validation — owned by #602.
* Analytical warehouse sizing and OLAP query performance — the analytics estate is a separate store by architectural rule and is not scaled here.
* Forecasting future storage and IOPS requirements — owned by #604.

---

## Recommended Solution

**Connection topology.** Insert PgBouncer as a sidecar-free deployment in front of the CloudNativePG read-write and read-only services, in transaction pooling mode. Transaction mode is the only mode that meaningfully multiplexes, and it forbids session-level state, so GORM must be configured with `PreferSimpleProtocol: true` on the pgx driver — otherwise server-side prepared statements collide across pooled sessions and produce intermittent `prepared statement "lrupsc_1_0" already exists` errors that are notoriously hard to diagnose. Application-side pools shrink to 5 connections per replica; PgBouncer holds the real pool.

```
app replicas (N×5)  ->  pgbouncer (default_pool_size 40, transaction mode)  ->  postgres primary (max_connections 300)
                    ->  pgbouncer-ro                                        ->  replica-1, replica-2
```

**Read routing.** Extend the tenant-scoped data access layer — the same single choke point that enforces RLS — with an explicit read intent, so routing is a deliberate declaration at the call site and the default is safe.

```go
// Default is primary. Replica reads are opt-in and named.
ctx = dal.WithReadIntent(ctx, dal.ReplicaEligible) // worklists, reports, catalogues
ctx = dal.WithReadIntent(ctx, dal.StrongRead)      // medication list, allergy list, dispatch state
```

Read-your-writes is enforced by capturing `pg_current_wal_insert_lsn()` after each transaction commit, storing it in Redis against the session for a short window, and having the router either wait for the replica's `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()` to reach it or fall back to the primary. Clinical write-then-read paths never observe stale data; a stale allergy list is a patient-safety event, so `StrongRead` is mandatory on medication, allergy, order and dispatch reads regardless of load.

**Partitioning.**

```sql
CREATE TABLE observation (
  observation_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  tenant_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  patient_id      uuid NOT NULL,
  encounter_id    uuid,
  effective_at    timestamptz NOT NULL,
  code_system     text NOT NULL,
  code            text NOT NULL,
  value_quantity  numeric,
  value_unit      text,
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, effective_at, observation_id)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (effective_at);

CREATE INDEX ON observation (tenant_id, patient_id, effective_at DESC);
ALTER TABLE observation ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
```

The partition key is leading-time and the primary key includes `tenant_id` first, so both the RLS predicate and the common "latest observations for this patient" access pattern are index-served. Partitions are monthly, created three months ahead by a Temporal scheduled workflow rather than a cron job, so a failed creation is visible, retried and alertable instead of silently missed — a missing future partition is an insert failure on a clinical write path. Old partitions are detached rather than dropped, and their retention is governed by the classification-driven retention rules, not by this issue.

**Migration.** Existing tables are converted online using a shadow partitioned table, a trigger-based dual write, a backfill in bounded batches, and an atomic rename. `pg_repack` is used for index rebuilds. No migration step takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for longer than the configured `lock_timeout`, and every migration is reversible.

**Timeouts by role.** `clinical_app` gets `statement_timeout = 5s`, `reporting_app` gets `60s`, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 30s` everywhere. This is what prevents a report from holding a snapshot that blocks autovacuum and bloats the clinical tables.

**Events.** A monitoring consumer publishes `platform.db.replication_lag.exceeded` and `platform.db.pool.saturated` on NATS JetStream, consumed by the alerting path.

**Sequencing.** Depends on #595 for instrumentation, since replication lag and pool saturation must be visible before replicas are trusted with reads. Must land before #597, because the caching strategy's staleness budget is meaningless without a defined replica consistency policy, and before #601, which places standbys across zones on top of this replication topology.

**Risks.** Transaction pooling silently breaks anything relying on session state — advisory locks, `SET LOCAL` outside a transaction, `LISTEN/NOTIFY` — so an audit of session-dependent code is part of the work, and `LISTEN/NOTIFY` usage is replaced with JetStream. Partition-key immutability means an `effective_at` correction becomes a delete-and-insert across partitions; this is handled explicitly in the data access layer rather than left to GORM. Replication lag under heavy write load is the residual risk against stale reads, bounded by the LSN wait with a hard timeout that falls back to the primary rather than serving stale clinical data.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a tenant with 400 million partitioned observation rows and the API tier autoscaled to 60 replicas under peak OPD load
**When** sustained clinical read and write traffic runs for one hour
**Then** total PostgreSQL backends stay below 70% of `max_connections`, no connection is refused, queries for a named patient's latest observations use an index scan against no more than two partitions, and p95 query time for that access pattern is at or below 50 ms.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** a read replica lagging 8 seconds behind the primary after a bulk import
**When** a doctor saves a progress note and immediately reloads the encounter, and separately a nurse opens an active medication list
**Then** the progress-note read is routed to the primary via the stored write LSN and returns the just-written note, the medication list is served from the primary because it is classified `StrongRead` and is never replica-eligible, replica-eligible worklist reads continue to be served from the lagging replica, and `platform.db.replication_lag.exceeded` is published.

### Edge Cases

* The scheduled partition-creation workflow fails: the failure alerts before the current partition's boundary is reached, and a clinical insert never fails because a future partition is missing.
* PgBouncer is restarted during peak traffic: in-flight transactions fail fast with a retryable error, the application retries idempotent reads, and no partial write is committed.
* A reporting query exceeds its 60-second statement timeout while holding a snapshot: it is cancelled, autovacuum on the clinical tables is unblocked, and the report surfaces a timeout to the user rather than hanging.
* A tenant is migrated from shared schema to database-per-tenant: RLS-enforced isolation is verified adversarially on the destination before cutover, and the source rows are only removed after a verified row-count and checksum match.
* A query on a partitioned table omits the partition key: the plan check in CI fails the build, because scanning every partition of `observation` is the regression this work exists to prevent.
* An RLS policy change alters a query plan from index scan to sequential scan on `audit_record`: the automated plan verification fails CI and blocks the merge.

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** the API tier scales to peak without a single refused database connection, clinical queries against multi-hundred-million-row tables remain index-served, and no user ever reads stale clinical data after their own write.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** the platform can onboard a multi-hospital group without a database re-architecture, and enterprise tenants demanding physical separation have a rehearsed migration path rather than a promise.
* **Success metric or validation method:** zero `too many clients` errors across a 12-week window; peak backend utilisation below 70% of `max_connections` under the #603 peak scenario; p95 at or below 50 ms for the patient-latest-observations pattern at 400 million rows; 100% of clinical write-then-read journeys returning fresh data under an injected 8-second replica lag, asserted by an integration test; zero sequential scans on partitioned clinical tables in the CI plan-verification suite; replication lag p99 under 2 seconds in steady state.
* **Monitoring period, where applicable:** 12 weeks post-deployment, tracking pool saturation, backend count, replication lag distribution, LSN-wait fallback rate to primary, partition count and size growth, autovacuum backlog, table and index bloat, and statement-timeout cancellations by connection role.

---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions

**Guardrail:** Accessibility and User Journey — the whole section.
**Reason:** the change is entirely below the API boundary — pooling, replication topology, partitioning, indexes and timeouts. No interface is added or altered, and no user-visible behaviour changes except that existing journeys remain fast under load.
**Alternative validation:** the critical clinical journeys affected by read routing — chart open after save, medication list, allergy list, dispatch state — are covered end to end by Playwright scenarios executed against an environment with deliberately injected replica lag, asserting the user sees their own writes. This validates the journey without an accessibility claim that does not apply.
**Residual risk:** none material to accessibility. The residual risk is behavioural, not interface-level: a misclassified read intent could route a clinical read to a replica, which is mitigated by the default being primary and by `StrongRead` being mandatory and test-enforced on the named clinical reads.
**Approved by:** Head of Platform Engineering and the Clinical Safety Officer, to be recorded on the pull request.

---

**Guardrail:** Code Quality — "Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved."
**Reason:** moving to PgBouncer transaction pooling deliberately removes support for session-scoped database state. Code using advisory locks, session-level `SET`, or `LISTEN/NOTIFY` will change behaviour, and that change is intended rather than incidental.
**Alternative validation:** a full audit of session-dependent database usage is completed and recorded on the pull request, with each occurrence either removed, converted to a transaction-scoped equivalent, or migrated to NATS JetStream. An integration suite runs the affected paths through PgBouncer in transaction mode to prove the replacements behave correctly under connection multiplexing.
**Residual risk:** an unaudited third-party library could rely on session state and fail intermittently under pooling. Mitigated by running the full integration suite through the pooler in staging for two weeks before production cutover, and by the ability to switch a specific service back to session pooling as a contained rollback.
**Approved by:** Head of Platform Engineering, to be recorded on the pull request.

items.title: ISS-0768: Letflow.Identity.RoleRegistry never threads tenant-schema prefix -- POST /roles always 500s (relation groups/tenant_role does not exist)
items.body:
Discovered live by a peer ai-dala-infra session (T-0140, seeding SwiftRoute tenant-persona QA users) attempting POST /roles against qa.bizdala.com. lib/letflow/identity/role_registry.ex never threads opts :: [prefix: String.t()] through its Repo calls (upsert_role/2, list_roles/0), unlike every other identity module which follows this established REQ-063/REQ-073 convention (lib/letflow/plugs/auth_pipeline.ex, lib/letflow/identity.ex provision_oidc_user/4 and list_effective_role_names/2). RoleRegistry always queries the default public schema, which has no groups/tenant_role tables (schema-per-tenant multitenancy). Confirmed via direct source grep, not version skew (deployed git ref vs local differ by one unrelated commit, role_registry.ex byte-identical). Net effect: POST /roles (and possibly GET /roles, list_roles/0) can never succeed for ANY tenant, on any deployment -- this is a real, systemic multitenancy bug, not specific to one tenant or QA. Blocks the tenant-admin GUIs role-management screen for every tenant that has never had a role successfully created (verify blast radius: is this a regression, or has RoleRegistry never worked since it shipped?). Affected: lib/letflow/identity/role_registry.ex, lib/letflow/routers/identity.ex (POST /roles, GET /roles routes).

Acceptance criteria:
- upsert_role/2 and list_roles/0 accept and correctly thread a required prefix opt through every Repo call, matching the established opts :: [prefix: String.t()] convention (REQ-063/REQ-073)
- the callers in lib/letflow/routers/identity.ex (POST /roles, GET /roles handlers) are updated to pass the caller's own tenant schema prefix, derived the same way other tenant-scoped routes in this router already do
- a real test creates a role for one tenant and confirms it is queryable only in that tenants own schema (not visible via a different tenants prefix, not written to public)
- investigate and record in the fix/PR whether this is a regression (RoleRegistry worked before some change) or has been broken since it shipped -- bounds the blast radius of any prior GET/POST /roles success claims
- mix letflow.check passes, with real output quoted

items.title: Tenant fan-out: one environment over many databases or schemas
items.body:
## Problem

A product with a schema or database per tenant has to apply the same migrations to hundreds of targets. Today that means one profile per tenant and one pipeline job each, with an approval per tenant.

## Proposal

- An environment can be a unit set: a profile template plus a tenant list (static, a file, or a SQL query run with the reader at plan time). Each unit keeps its own history.
- A wave over a unit set has one gate bound to a set digest of every unit's plan; a deciding job records per-unit digests; share jobs apply subsets and refuse a unit whose plan moved since the decision; re-running continues with the units that did not finish.
- One plan comment groups identical plans across units and lists outliers.

## Done when

- Claim `tenant-wave` passes and is caught on Postgres schemas and ClickHouse databases.
- A bench in `bench/` for N tenants records fan-out time and comment size.

## Proof

Prove it with the scenario claims, rolled up (#39): the `waves` claim (a tenant part). Every part fails under BREAK=1 on its own.

Roadmap rank 17 of 30.

items.body:
## Situation

Row-level security (#26) on a shared schema is the right default, and it will not close every enterprise deal. Large hospital groups and government-linked institutions routinely require physical separation of their data as a procurement condition — their information-security questionnaire asks whether their records sit in the same tables as another organisation's, and "yes, but with policies" fails the question regardless of how sound the policies are. The architecture brief accordingly names schema-per-tenant and database-per-tenant as premium tiers.

Nothing supports this today. The data-access layer resolves one connection pool to one database with one `public` schema. If a tenant needed a separate schema or a separate database, there is no catalogue to look it up in, no routing to reach it, no way to run a migration across a variable set of targets, and no way for a NATS consumer or Temporal activity to reach the right database for the tenant on the message.

Affected: the enterprise sales motion, which currently has no answer to the separation question; the platform operations team, who would otherwise face manually managed one-off databases with divergent schema versions; the hospital admin at a separated tenant, who must see identical product behaviour; and the DPO, since data residency is a hard boundary and physical separation interacts directly with residency commitments.

This issue builds the isolation-mode framework — catalogue, routing, migration orchestration and observability — so that a tenant's storage topology becomes a configurable property rather than a fork of the platform. Issue #28 then productises the strongest mode as a commercial tier.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** platform engineer and as any product module
**I want** a tenant's storage topology — shared schema, dedicated schema, or dedicated database — to be a property resolved from a catalogue and applied transparently by the data-access layer
**So that** the same application code serves every tenant regardless of isolation mode, and schema changes reach every target reliably.

### Scope

**In scope**

* An `isolation_mode` property per tenant: `shared_schema`, `dedicated_schema`, `dedicated_database`, held in a control-plane tenant catalogue that is itself never tenant-partitioned.
* A connection resolver: given tenant context (#25), return the correct pool and, for `dedicated_schema`, set the `search_path` for the transaction alongside `app.tenant_id`.
* Bounded per-tenant pooling with a shared-pool fallback, so a hundred dedicated tenants do not exhaust database connections; pools are lazily created, idle-evicted and capped.
* Migration orchestration: a single logical migration version applied across all targets — the shared database, every dedicated schema and every dedicated database — as a Temporal workflow with per-target status, retry and resumability, plus a hard gate preventing application deploys when any target lags the required version.
* Schema-version reporting: an operational view showing every target's applied version and drift.
* RLS retained in every mode. A dedicated schema or database still carries `tenant_id` and its policies; separation is defence in depth, not a replacement.
* Event consumers and Temporal activities resolve the target from the same catalogue, so no execution path assumes the shared pool.
* Health, latency and connection metrics tagged by isolation mode and target.

**Out of scope**

* The commercial dedicated-database tier, entitlement and provisioning of new clusters — issue #28, which consumes this framework.
* Migrating an existing shared tenant's data into a separated target — issue #28 owns the cutover workflow.
* Country-level residency routing and regional deployments — the Country Profile epic; residency selects the region, this issue selects the target within it.
* Per-tenant encryption keys and isolated backups — the Data Isolation encryption and backup stories.
* Read-replica routing and analytics offload — the OLAP separation story.

---

## Recommended Solution

Introduce a control-plane catalogue and make the connection resolver the only component that knows about topology.

```sql
-- control plane; not tenant-partitioned, platform role only
CREATE TABLE tenant_storage (
  tenant_id      uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  isolation_mode text NOT NULL
      CHECK (isolation_mode IN ('shared_schema','dedicated_schema','dedicated_database')),
  region         text NOT NULL,                  -- residency boundary
  cluster_ref    text NOT NULL,                  -- CloudNativePG cluster name
  database_name  text NOT NULL,
  schema_name    text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'public',
  schema_version bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  status         text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active', -- provisioning|active|migrating|readonly|retired
  secret_ref     text NOT NULL,                  -- vault path for credentials
  updated_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT schema_matches_mode CHECK (
    (isolation_mode = 'dedicated_schema') = (schema_name <> 'public')
    OR isolation_mode = 'dedicated_database')
);
```

Credentials are never stored here — only a vault reference, consistent with the secrets rule.

The resolver sits underneath the `Do` provider from #25, so callers are unchanged:

```go
func (p *Provider) Do(ctx context.Context, fn func(*gorm.DB) error) error {
    tc, err := FromContext(ctx); if err != nil { return ErrNoTenantContext }
    tgt, err := p.catalogue.Resolve(ctx, tc.TenantID)   // Redis-cached, NATS-invalidated
    if err != nil { return err }
    if tgt.Status == StatusMigrating { return ErrTenantReadOnly }
    db, err := p.pools.Get(tgt)                          // bounded, lazily created
    if err != nil { return err }
    return db.WithContext(ctx).Transaction(func(tx *gorm.DB) error {
        if err := tx.Exec("SET LOCAL search_path = ?", tgt.SchemaName).Error; err != nil { return err }
        if err := tx.Exec("SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = ?", tc.TenantID).Error; err != nil { return err }
        return fn(tx)
    })
}
```

`search_path` is set with `SET LOCAL` for the same reason as `app.tenant_id` — a pooled connection must not carry it beyond the transaction. Setting both in one place means no module can get one without the other.

Pool management is the main operational risk. Each dedicated database gets a small pool (default 5, configurable per tenant through #23); pools are created on first use, evicted after 15 minutes idle, and the total across all pools is capped with a metric and alert at 80% of the cap. Dedicated *schemas* share the underlying cluster pool and cost nothing extra in connections, which is why `dedicated_schema` is the recommended middle tier.

Migration orchestration runs as a Temporal workflow, `SchemaMigrationWorkflow`, because it is long-running, must survive worker restarts and needs per-target retry:

```
MigrateAll(version) →
  fan out over tenant_storage targets (bounded parallelism, default 8)
    → per target: advisory lock, apply migration, update schema_version, emit progress
  → on any target failure: continue others, mark target degraded, do not roll back succeeded targets
  → completion: assert all active targets at target version
```

Migrations must therefore be backward-compatible and additive within a release — expand/contract only — because targets are transiently at different versions. The deploy gate enforces this from the other side: the application refuses to start if `min(schema_version)` across active targets is below its required minimum.

API surface (platform-only):

```
GET  /internal/tenant-storage                      (catalogue, filterable by mode/status)
GET  /internal/tenant-storage/{tenant_id}
POST /internal/tenant-storage/{tenant_id}/mode     { isolation_mode }  -- registers intent; cutover is #28
GET  /internal/schema-migrations/status            (per-target version and drift)
POST /internal/schema-migrations/run               { version }
GET  /internal/tenant-storage/pools                (pool utilisation by target)
```

Events:

```json
// platform.tenant_storage.changed
{ "tenant_id":"…", "isolation_mode":"dedicated_schema",
  "cluster_ref":"hms-in-prod-2", "schema_name":"t_9f2a", "status":"active" }
// platform.schema_migration.target_completed
{ "target":"hms-in-prod-2/hms/t_9f2a", "version":184, "duration_ms":9120 }
```

`platform.tenant_storage.changed` invalidates the resolver cache across every pod and every consumer, so routing converges without a restart.

OpenFGA — the catalogue is platform infrastructure and no tenant user may read it:

```
type tenant_storage
  relations
    define platform_operator: [user, service#member]
    define can_read: platform_operator
    define can_change_mode: [user, role#assignee] and platform_operator
```

Sequencing: depends on #25 (context and provider) and #26 (RLS, which stays on in all modes). Blocks #28. The Country Profile epic must define `region` semantics before dedicated targets are provisioned outside India.

Risks: (a) connection exhaustion as dedicated tenants grow — mitigated by bounded, idle-evicted pools, the utilisation alert, and steering most customers to `dedicated_schema`; (b) schema drift leaving one hospital on an old version — mitigated by the drift view, the deploy gate and an alert on any active target more than one version behind; (c) a resolver cache serving a stale target during a mode change — mitigated by `status = migrating` forcing read-only and by NATS invalidation on every catalogue change.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** three tenants configured as `shared_schema`, `dedicated_schema` and `dedicated_database` in the same region
**When** the identical application code path serves an equivalent request for each
**Then** each request is routed to its correct cluster, database and schema, `app.tenant_id` and `search_path` are both set within the transaction, results are identical in shape, RLS remains active in all three modes, and traces carry `isolation_mode` and `cluster_ref` attributes.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** a tenant whose dedicated database cluster is unreachable — pod eviction or network partition
**When** a request for that tenant arrives
**Then** the resolver fails after a bounded connection timeout, the request returns `503` with a retry hint, no request is silently routed to the shared database, other tenants are entirely unaffected, and a `tenant_target_unavailable` alert fires identifying the cluster and tenant.

### Edge Cases

* A schema migration where one dedicated target fails mid-run — the workflow completes the remaining targets, marks the failed one degraded, is resumable from the failure point, and never leaves a partially applied migration on that target.
* Total pool count reaches the configured cap — new dedicated targets fail fast with a clear operational error and an alert, rather than starving existing pools of connections.
* A tenant in `status = migrating` receives a write — rejected with `ErrTenantReadOnly` and a user-visible maintenance message; reads continue to be served.
* A NATS consumer receives an event for a dedicated-database tenant while its resolver cache is cold — the resolver loads from the catalogue on demand; the message is redelivered rather than dead-lettered if the target is temporarily unavailable.
* A dedicated schema name collides with an existing schema — generation uses a tenant-derived prefix with a uniqueness constraint at the catalogue level, and provisioning fails before any DDL runs.
* A tenant is retired — its target moves to `readonly` then `retired`; pools are closed, the catalogue row is retained for audit, and requests return `410` rather than routing to a deleted database.
## Engineering Guardrails

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** a tenant's storage topology is a catalogue property; the same application code serves shared-schema, dedicated-schema and dedicated-database tenants with identical behaviour, and schema changes reach every target with visible per-target status.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** the enterprise separation requirement can be answered concretely, and operations gains a single view of schema version across all targets instead of managing one-off databases by hand.

items.body:
## Situation

The platform is greenfield. There is no single place where a field is declared to be PHI, PII, sensitive, operational or analytical, and no machine-readable mapping from those classifications to the controls that must apply (encryption, access rule, retention period, export eligibility, analytics eligibility). Today every service would decide independently whether a column may leave the operational database, appear in a log line, be copied to the OLAP warehouse, or be included in a subject-access export. That is exactly how PHI leaks into dashboards and log aggregators.

This affects everyone downstream: the DPO, who cannot answer "where does this data live and what protects it" without reading source code; the compliance team, who must produce evidence for NABH audits and for tenant security questionnaires; and every backend engineer, who currently has no authoritative answer to "may I put this field in an event payload?".

MediCore, MediConnect, LabConnect and PharmaConnect all handle clinical data, but the concrete legal instrument varies by tenant and country — DPDP Act 2023 for India (issue #57), HIPAA for a future US deployment (#58), GDPR for EU (#59). The controls those regimes demand overlap heavily: classify data, encrypt it, restrict access on a need-to-know basis, log access tamper-evidently, retain it for a defined period, delete it on a defined trigger, and notify on breach. This issue builds that shared control baseline once, so the regime-specific issues become configuration and evidence rather than three parallel implementations.

Without it, #57, #58 and #59 each reimplement classification and each drifts.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** Data Protection Officer and as a platform engineer
**I want** every persisted field classified in a machine-readable registry that drives encryption, access, logging, retention and export controls
**So that** privacy obligations are enforced by the platform rather than by developer memory, and evidence can be produced on demand.

### Scope

**In scope**

* A data classification registry: every table and column in the operational schema tagged `phi`, `pii`, `sensitive`, `operational` or `analytical`, with a purpose and a lawful-basis hint.
* A control matrix mapping each classification to required controls: encryption at rest, whether the field may appear in a NATS JetStream event payload, whether it may be replicated to OLAP, log-redaction behaviour, default retention class.
* A Go struct-tag convention (`privacy:"phi,retention=clinical_10y"`) plus a CI check that fails the build if a GORM model has an untagged field, or if a tagged PHI field is serialised into an event schema not on the allow-list.
* Automatic redaction in the shared logging/OpenTelemetry middleware driven by the registry — PHI and sensitive fields are hashed or dropped before a log or span attribute is emitted.
* A field-level encryption helper for the `sensitive` class (Aadhaar-derived tokens, government identifiers) using envelope encryption with per-tenant data keys.
* An `AdminConnect` read-only compliance view rendering the registry: field, classification, stores it lands in, retention class, last reviewed.
* Registry export as a signed artefact for use as audit evidence and to seed the GDPR Article 30 record (#59).

**Out of scope**

* DPDP notice, grievance and breach-reporting workflow — owned by #57.
* HIPAA BAA register and minimum-necessary role mapping — owned by #58.
* GDPR lawful-basis register, DPIA and transfer mechanism — owned by #59.
* Consent capture and artefact lifecycle — owned by #60; this issue only records which classifications are consent-gated.
* Execution of deletion and retention jobs — owned by #63; this issue defines the retention classes those jobs consume.

---

## Recommended Solution

Implement the registry as first-class data in PostgreSQL 16, not as a spreadsheet, so it can be queried by services and by CI.

```sql
CREATE TABLE data_classification (
  id              uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  schema_name     text NOT NULL,
  table_name      text NOT NULL,
  column_name     text NOT NULL,
  classification  text NOT NULL
    CHECK (classification IN ('phi','pii','sensitive','operational','analytical')),
  purpose         text NOT NULL,
  retention_class text NOT NULL REFERENCES retention_class(code),
  event_emittable boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  olap_eligible   boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  log_action      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'drop'
    CHECK (log_action IN ('drop','hash','mask_last4','allow')),
  reviewed_by     uuid, reviewed_at timestamptz,
  UNIQUE (schema_name, table_name, column_name)
);

CREATE TABLE retention_class (
  code text PRIMARY KEY,          -- clinical_10y, billing_8y, session_90d, ephemeral_24h
  min_retention interval NOT NULL,
  max_retention interval,
  legal_basis   text NOT NULL,
  deletable_on_request boolean NOT NULL
);
```

The registry is a control-plane table (feature/config data, not PHI), so it is not tenant-scoped; the country profile can override `retention_class` per country via a `retention_class_override(country_code, code, min_retention)` table, satisfying the country-profile rule rather than branching on `country == "IN"`.

Enforcement runs at three points:

1. **Build time.** A `go vet`-style analyser walks all GORM models, reconciles struct fields against `data_classification`, and fails CI on any unclassified field or on a PHI field referenced by an event schema whose subject is not in the allow-list. This is the single most valuable control because it prevents drift.
2. **Runtime, on emission.** The shared logging and OTel exporters consult a registry snapshot cached in Redis (`privacy:registry:v{n}`, refreshed on `DataClassificationChanged`) and apply `log_action` before the record leaves the process. Span attributes go through the same filter — traces are a common PHI leak path.
3. **Runtime, on replication.** The OLAP change-data-capture sink drops any column where `olap_eligible = false`, so the analytics warehouse cannot receive identifiable PHI by accident. This is the mechanical enforcement of the OLTP/OLAP separation rule.

Field-level encryption for `sensitive` uses envelope encryption: a per-tenant data encryption key wrapped by a KMS key, with the wrapped key stored in `tenant_crypto_key`. Keeping keys per tenant makes crypto-shredding a viable erasure mechanism for #63 and is a hard dependency for it — land this issue first.

API surface (AdminConnect, DPO role only):

```
GET  /api/v1/privacy/classifications?table=&classification=
GET  /api/v1/privacy/classifications/{id}
PUT  /api/v1/privacy/classifications/{id}      # requires dual approval
GET  /api/v1/privacy/retention-classes
POST /api/v1/privacy/registry/export           # signed evidence bundle
GET  /api/v1/privacy/coverage                  # % of columns classified
```

Events published: `DataClassificationChanged` (invalidates the Redis snapshot and the CDC column filter) and `PrivacyRegistryExported` (audit trail).

OpenFGA model — the registry is a governance object, not clinical data, so relations are narrow:

```
type privacy_registry
  relations
    define viewer: [user, role#member]
    define editor: [role#member]
    define approver: [role#member]   # dual control: editor != approver
```

`PUT` requires a second principal holding `approver` before the change takes effect; the change is staged in `data_classification_pending` until approved. Reclassifying a field from `phi` to `operational` is the obvious attack path — dual control plus a permanent audit record is the mitigation.

Sequencing: this issue has no upstream dependency and blocks #57, #58, #59 and #63. Consent (#60) can proceed in parallel.

Principal risks. First, the CI analyser producing so much noise that teams disable it — mitigate by seeding the registry from the existing schema with an explicit `unclassified` backlog and enforcing the gate only on new and changed models for the first two sprints. Second, the Redis snapshot going stale and PHI reaching logs — mitigate with a version counter checked on every process start and a fail-closed default (`log_action = 'drop'`) when the snapshot is unavailable. Third, performance of per-field redaction in hot paths — the filter is a precomputed field-index map, not reflection, and is benchmarked as part of the acceptance threshold.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a GORM model field classified as `phi` with `log_action = 'drop'`
**When** a service logs a struct containing that field and emits an OTel span with it as an attribute
**Then** neither the log record nor the exported span contains the value, the field is absent rather than empty-stringed, and the surrounding diagnostic context is preserved.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** the Redis registry snapshot is unavailable and no local cache is warm
**When** a service attempts to emit a log line or replicate a row to OLAP
**Then** the platform fails closed — all non-`operational` fields are dropped, a `privacy_registry_unavailable` metric is incremented, and the OLAP sink pauses rather than replicating unfiltered rows.

### Edge Cases

* A developer adds a new column to a GORM model without a `privacy` tag — CI fails with the exact file, struct and field name.
* A JSONB column (for example a FHIR `Observation` payload) holds mixed classifications — the registry supports JSON-path level entries and the redactor walks them.
* A field is reclassified from `sensitive` to `pii` — the pending change is visible to the editor but has no runtime effect until an approver who is not the editor confirms it.
* An engineer with `viewer` but not `editor` calls `PUT /api/v1/privacy/classifications/{id}` — 403, and the attempt is written to the tamper-evident audit log.
* A tenant on the schema-per-tenant premium tier — the registry resolves classification by logical table name, not physical schema, so all tenant schemas are covered by one entry.
* Retention class override exists for a country profile but the base class does not — write is rejected by the foreign key rather than silently defaulting.

---

---

## Result

* Expected user or system outcome: every persisted column carries a classification, and redaction, OLAP eligibility and retention are derived from it automatically.
* Expected business or operational outcome: the DPO can answer a tenant security questionnaire or an accreditation query from the registry export without engineering involvement.
* Success metric or validation method: 100% of columns in the operational schema classified with zero `unclassified` entries at merge; zero PHI-classified values found by the log-scanner probe across a 7-day sample of production logs and traces; redaction adds no more than 0.4 ms to p95 request latency measured against the MediCore OPD endpoint.

items.body:
## Situation

The platform will hold patient records, prescriptions, lab results and pharmacy dispensing history for many unrelated hospitals, laboratories and pharmacies in the same PostgreSQL 16 cluster. Today there is no isolation mechanism at all: any handler that forgets a `WHERE tenant_id = ?` clause would return another hospital's patients. In healthcare that is not a bug, it is a reportable data breach — under the **DPDP Act 2023** the platform, acting as Data Processor, would have to notify the affected Data Fiduciaries and the Data Protection Board, and under **CERT-In** directions the incident must be reported within the mandated window with retained logs to support the investigation.

Relying on developer discipline is not a control. Across eleven products and hundreds of endpoints, a single missed predicate in a reporting query, an admin export, a background reconciliation job or a `Raw()` GORM call is enough. The affected parties are every patient on the platform, every hospital admin whose accreditation (**NABH**) and every laboratory whose **NABL** status depends on demonstrable confidentiality controls, and the DPO who must be able to state, with evidence, that cross-tenant access is structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely.

There is a second dimension: some enterprise hospital groups will contractually require physical separation and will not accept a shared schema. The isolation design must therefore support shared-schema row-level security as the default and schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant as premium tiers, without every module knowing which mode it is running in.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** platform engineer building any HMS module
**I want** tenant isolation enforced by the database and a single tenant-scoped data-access layer rather than by per-query discipline
**So that** no application code path — including reports, exports, background jobs and ad-hoc queries — can read or write another tenant's data even if the developer forgets.

### Scope

**In scope**

* PostgreSQL row-level security enabled and forced on every tenant-owned table, with `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` policies bound to a session-scoped tenant setting.
* A single tenant-scoped data-access layer in Go that acquires a connection, sets the tenant context inside the transaction, and is the only supported way to obtain a `*gorm.DB`.
* Gin middleware that resolves the tenant from the authenticated principal's claims (never from a client-supplied header) and fails closed when absent.
* A migration lint that fails CI if a new table carrying a `tenant_id` column ships without RLS enabled, forced and policied.
* Object-storage isolation: per-tenant key prefixes and signed URLs scoped to that prefix with a short expiry.
* Isolation mode abstraction so `shared_rls`, `schema` and `database` modes are resolved by connection routing without module-level branching.
* An adversarial cross-tenant test suite executed in CI: for every read and write endpoint, attempt access with a valid token from tenant B against tenant A's resource identifiers.
* NATS JetStream subject and consumer naming that carries the tenant so no subscriber receives another tenant's events.
* Per-tenant connection-pool and query cost limits to contain noisy neighbours.

**Out of scope**

* The tenant registry and lifecycle itself — owned by *Tenant management* (#13).
* Per-tenant encryption keys, isolated backup streams and export controls — tracked separately in the Data Isolation epic.
* Country-level residency partitioning and regional deployment topology — a separate infrastructure decision above tenancy.
* Relationship-based clinical authorisation (which clinician may see which patient *within* a tenant) — owned by the OpenFGA care-relationship model.
* Analytics/OLAP isolation; the warehouse holds de-identified aggregates only and is governed by its own epic.

---

## Recommended Solution

Treat the database as the enforcement point and the data-access layer as the only gate, then prove it adversarially.

### Row-level security

Every tenant-owned table carries a non-null `tenant_id uuid REFERENCES tenant(id)`. Applications connect as a role that is **not** the table owner and does **not** hold `BYPASSRLS`:

```sql
ALTER TABLE patient ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE patient FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY patient_tenant_read ON patient FOR SELECT
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('hms.tenant_id', true)::uuid);

CREATE POLICY patient_tenant_write ON patient FOR ALL
  USING      (tenant_id = current_setting('hms.tenant_id', true)::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('hms.tenant_id', true)::uuid);
```

The `WITH CHECK` clause is essential — without it a tenant could insert or update a row *into* another tenant. `current_setting(..., true)` returning NULL evaluates the predicate to NULL, which denies rather than permits, so an unset context fails closed.

### Tenant-scoped data-access layer

```go
// The only way to obtain a handle. No exported *gorm.DB elsewhere.
func (r *Runtime) WithTenant(ctx context.Context, fn func(tx *gorm.DB) error) error {
    tid, ok := tenantctx.From(ctx)
    if !ok { return ErrNoTenantContext }
    return r.route(tid).Transaction(func(tx *gorm.DB) error {
        if err := tx.Exec("SELECT set_config('hms.tenant_id', ?, true)", tid).Error; err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return fn(tx)
    })
}
```

`set_config(..., true)` scopes the setting to the transaction, so a pooled connection returned to PgBouncer cannot leak context into the next request. `route(tid)` resolves the isolation mode from a Redis-cached tenant descriptor and returns the shared pool, a schema-qualified pool, or a dedicated pool — the only place isolation mode is known.

A `go vet`-style custom analyser plus an architecture test fail the build if any package outside the runtime imports `gorm.io/gorm` and constructs a session directly, or calls `Raw`/`Exec` outside `WithTenant`.

### Tenant resolution

Gin middleware reads the `tenant_id` claim from the Keycloak-issued token, cross-checks it against the OpenFGA `can_access` relation for the requested tenant object, and injects it into the context. A `X-Tenant-Id` request header is accepted only for platform operators holding `operator` on `platform`, and that path is separately audited.

```
type tenant
  relations
    define member: [user, service_account]
    define admin: [user]
    define can_access: member or admin or operator from platform
```

### Adversarial testing

A table-driven suite enumerates the OpenAPI surface, seeds two tenants with identical-shaped fixtures, and for each operation issues tenant B's token against tenant A's resource id. Anything other than 403/404 fails the build. A second suite runs raw SQL as the application role with `hms.tenant_id` unset and asserts zero rows from every RLS-protected table. Both run in CI on every pull request and nightly against a synthetic-data environment; PHI never appears in non-production.

### Events and storage

JetStream subjects are `hms.{country}.{tenant_id}.{domain}.{event}` with durable consumers filtered by tenant, so a misconfigured subscriber cannot wildcard across tenants. Object keys are `{tenant_id}/{domain}/{object_id}`; signed URLs are minted only by the storage service after an OpenFGA check and expire in 15 minutes.

### Sequencing and risks

Depends on #13 for `tenant.id` and on Keycloak claim mapping. The main risks are: a superuser or migration role bypassing RLS — mitigated by `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` and a separate, non-owning application role; connection pooling leaking context — mitigated by transaction-local `set_config` and a pool test that interleaves two tenants on one connection; and RLS predicate cost on large tables — mitigated by composite indexes leading with `tenant_id` and a query-plan regression check on the highest-traffic clinical reads.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** two active tenants, a ward nurse authenticated against tenant A, and patient records existing in both
**When** the nurse lists patients through any MediCore endpoint
**Then** only tenant A's records are returned, the executed statement carries `hms.tenant_id` set to tenant A inside the transaction, and the same query run without that setting returns zero rows.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** a valid, unexpired token issued to a pathologist in tenant B
**When** that token is used to request a diagnostic report belonging to tenant A by its exact identifier
**Then** the request is rejected with 404 (not 403, to avoid confirming existence), no row is returned, the RLS policy denies at the database layer even if the handler's predicate were removed, and an audit record of the attempted cross-tenant access is written with the principal, tenant pair and resource type.

### Edge Cases

* A background reconciliation job runs with no HTTP request context — it must enumerate tenants explicitly and open one `WithTenant` scope per tenant; an unscoped run fails fast rather than reading everything.
* A connection is returned to the pool mid-request and reused by another tenant — transaction-local settings must prevent any bleed; covered by an interleaved-connection test.
* A new table is added in a migration with a `tenant_id` column but no policy — CI migration lint fails the pull request.
* A tenant in `database` isolation mode is queried through the shared pool — the router must refuse rather than silently fall back to shared RLS.
* A signed object-storage URL for tenant A is replayed by a user in tenant B before expiry — the storage service re-checks the prefix and rejects.
* A JetStream consumer is created with a wildcard subject spanning tenants — rejected by the consumer-provisioning helper.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** cross-tenant data access is structurally impossible; a forgotten predicate produces zero rows rather than another hospital's patients.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** the platform can evidence its confidentiality controls to hospital procurement, NABH and NABL assessors, and to enterprise groups evaluating the premium isolation tiers.
* **Success metric or validation method:** 100% of tenant-owned tables have RLS enabled and forced, verified by an automated catalogue assertion; the adversarial suite covers at least 95% of authenticated endpoints with zero cross-tenant successes; p95 latency on the top ten clinical read queries increases by no more than 5% against the pre-RLS baseline.
* **Monitoring period:** continuous — the catalogue assertion and adversarial suite run nightly; a 30-day latency watch follows the first production rollout.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
